added.text: **The effective dictionary is a public API.** AGS4 Rule 18 makes the dictionary a file validates against the standard dictionary ∪ the file's own DICT group — and until now that union existed only as two private copies inside the validator, so a read-only consumer could not build it without pulling in the rule engine or writing a third copy. The one shared implementation now lives in `laterite-ags4-reference::effective_dict`: `FileDict` reads every column a DICT row can declare (`DICT_GRP`, `DICT_HDNG`, `DICT_STAT`, `DICT_DTYP`, `DICT_UNIT`, plus `DICT_PGRP` from GROUP-type rows), tolerantly — malformed DICT contributes nothing, because reporting it stays Rule 18's job — and `EffectiveDict` layers it over a standard edition. `laterite-ags4-core` re-exports the module with an adapter for its own read codec, so a reader that depends on core alone can bind a file-declared group's columns, statuses, units and parent. The validator's Rule 7/9, 10a–c and 19b families all consume the shared module now; both private copies are deleted, and python-ags4 parity held by identity across the rewire. (#777)

**The release report now says which stamped crate versions never reached crates.io.** `release_status.py` derived everything from this tree and nothing from a registry, so the only notion of *released* it had was *stamped here* — and those are not the same thing. `laterite-ags4-emit` 0.12.0 was stamped, recorded in the release notes as the first per-crate publish, and absent from crates.io, with nothing in the repo able to tell: the tree was self-consistent, so no gate had anything to disagree with, and publishing is not a repo change, so no diff existed for one to fire on. The report asks now, per crate, against the sparse index `cargo` itself resolves against — so *present there* is exactly *a consumer can depend on it* — and carries a `crates.io` column plus a `PUBLISH OWED` verdict beside the bump verdict, because a bump owed and a publish owed are different actions by different people and one was masking the other. Reading a registry introduces the failure a nag must not have, so **unreachable is its own state the whole way to the render**: it shouts nothing, is never folded into *unpublished*, and the count of crates that went unasked prints on every run, pass or quiet — a report that cried publish-owed over a lost DNS lookup would get switched off, and the real one with it. `publish_crates.py::on_registry` collapses every failure to *no* for the opposite and equally correct reason: it retries, so both answers mean wait. A yanked stamp is its own state too, because crates.io is append-only and that number can never be published again — it needs a human and a new number, not a publish run. `--no-registry` skips the read for an offline run and says so, rather than leaving the column silently blank. PyPI and npm are still not read, so the product tier keeps its half of the blind spot, and the footer says which half that is (#801).

**The engine release cut derives itself nightly.** `release_status.py` now measures each published crate from the exact commit its crates.io tarball was built from (never a stamp that went nowhere), reads the requirement ranges the registry froze — the signal #809 proved invisible to every in-tree gate, where a moved dependency floor strands published crates that re-export it — and derives the owed act per crate: bump (0.x parts, never a major), publish, or needs-a-human. The nightly `engine-cut` job tracks the owed set on its own issue, auto-dispatches the approval-gated crates.io publish for anything stamped but absent, and (once promoted from answer-only via `ENGINE_CUT_MODE=pr`) opens the cut PR itself; a per-PR coherence gate fails any change that moves a floor past a published pin without bumping the pinning crates alongside.

**Each product surface records the engine versions it ships.** The four product surfaces (`laterite-py`, `laterite-node`, `laterite-cli`, `laterite-ags4-wasm`) now declare their published engine dependencies as `{ path, version }` — the path still wins locally, and the version turns the manifest at any product tag into the record of which engine versions that release shipped. `bump_crate.py` moves every member pin with the crate it bumps, a guard test holds the pins equal to each crate's own version, and cargo itself refuses a path crate a pin no longer admits. The last step of #781's per-crate sequence.

**The certificate says what the file defines.** A `.ags.idx` now carries `defines` — the sorted group codes the file's own `DICT` declares, read through the shared Rule 18 effective-dictionary implementation at mint time. One fetch of a remote file's cert tells a reader it carries non-standard groups and that `DICT` (which the byte index locates precisely) is where they are declared; the definitions themselves are deliberately not duplicated. Old certificates read back as "not measured" rather than "declares nothing" — the same honesty rule the per-tier coverage states follow. Exposed as `Sidecar.defines` on the Python and Node surfaces.

**`lat fix` repairs Rule 5's unquoted rows — when the repair is provable** (#778). A DATA row whose fields lost their quotes re-quotes losslessly exactly when it binds without excess fields (#776's discriminator): the row must not overflow the group's declared headings, must tokenize cleanly, and the re-quoted line must split back to the identical values — an invariant the engine checks per row, not a judgement. Overflowing rows (the genuinely ambiguous case: nothing can say which side of the comma the heading wanted), quote-mangled rows, and non-DATA rows stay declined and flagged. The fix is Safe (default), composes with Rule 4's short-row pad in one pass, and surfaces everywhere fixes do: `laterite.fix` (`FixableRule` gains `"5"`), the Node `fix()` union, the wasm Apply-Fixes types, and the `lat rules` Fix? column.

**File-declared groups mint `_id`/`_parent_id` from their own DICT declarations** (#815). The Rule 18 effective dictionary is now the READ side's identity authority for a group the standard registry does not know: `keychain::group_row_ids_effective` builds the id from the declared KEY tuple (`DICT_STAT`, the same declarations the validator keys Rule 10a off) and the declared parent (`DICT_PGRP`), so `child._parent_id == parent._id` holds across the registry/file boundary — adopted by the Python, Node and browser read surfaces together, so no surface invents identity alone. A standard group's ids are byte-identical to before (the file's DICT never re-keys it: identity must not fork per delivery file), and a group declaring no KEY headings stays unkeyed rather than stamping every row with the empty-chain id. `laterite-ags4-reference` 0.13.0 (the additive API), core 0.13.1 and diff 0.12.1 ride the moved floor.

**The Python-lane benchmark measures memory, and writes** (#821). `tools/bench-vs-python-ags4.py` grows a peak-RSS harness — each (library, axis, rung) memory cell is a fresh subprocess running one end-to-end operation through that library's public API, the same instrument on both sides — and a fourth axis: **write** (baseline `dataframe_to_AGS4`; ours through both doors, compat's streaming `dataframe_to_AGS4` and native `build_ags4`). Every run writes a machine-readable results file (`tools/perf-results/python-lane.json`, schema declared in the tool) carrying times, peak-RSS cells, the ×-of-output headline factor, the import-floor baselines and any refusals — a rung a side cannot run without swapping is recorded as a refusal, never skipped. Memory columns stop at the 265 MB rung; the 524 MB rung stays time-only (epic #820, decision 7).

changed.text: **emit's cell is its own enum, not a JSON value** (#790). `GroupInput.rows` carries `laterite_ags4_types::Cell` (`Null | Text | Int | Float | Bool`), and `ags4_str` takes it — one authority for AGS4 wire spelling, unchanged bytes (a differential test pins the float spellings to the `serde_json` renderings they replaced). A cell is only ever a scalar, but Cargo's feature unification let other crates' legitimate `preserve_order` swell `Value`'s unused `Map` variant — and with it every cell of every build — in every shipped binary; the browser's JSON door now deserialises straight into `Cell` with no `Value` intermediate, and `serde_json` is out of `laterite-ags4-emit`'s dependencies entirely, so the crate cannot grow a JSON-value hot path back without a manifest diff saying so. Breaking for `laterite-ags4-emit` (0.13.0) and `laterite-ags4-types` (0.12.0) on crates.io; the `laterite` facade's surface is byte-identical — its own `ags4::Cell` existed precisely to keep the engine's row type out of the public API. The measurements pricing this (the heap composition, the per-cell ladder) live on #788/#789/#790; design: `ags-wiki/design/dec-emit-cell-representation.md`.

**emit's Arrow door streams** (#790, part 2). `emit_ags4_from_arrow(Vec<ArrowGroup>, &EmitOpts)` formats each cell straight off its record batch into the wire string — no row-major input copy — and all three Arrow hosts (Python, Node, browser IPC) now enter through it; the #695 DT-precision rendering rides `opts.edition` unchanged. The transpose entry points (`cell_value`, `group_from_arrow`, `group_from_arrow_with_meta`, `group_from_arrow_with_meta_at_edition`) are retired from the public API (reliquary rows carry the receipts) — the type→cell mapping itself survives crate-internal, still one function for every host. The two doors now meet at the formatted group, held by a differential test that also pins their one intended divergence (typed temporals render at declared UNIT precision; caller strings emit verbatim). Breaking for `laterite-ags4-emit`, within the already-stamped 0.13.0. Measured A/B on the #790 workload lives on the issue.

**laterite-transport 0.11.1** — the patch bump the nightly engine cut derived (#813): the crate's code moved since its published 0.11.0 with no API movement, so the next publish stops skipping it by version identity. Version only; no behaviour change rides this entry.

**laterite-ags4-validator 0.13.0** — the Rule 5 fix adds a `FixKind` variant, a breaking change on the exhaustive public enum (the semver gate's verdict against the published 0.12.0), so the crate takes the 0.x minor. `laterite-ags4-emit` 0.13.1 and `laterite-ags4-trust` 0.13.1 ride along: their published pins froze `^0.12.0`, and the coherence gate holds that a moved floor may not strand a published crate (#809's class).

**compat's `dataframe_to_AGS4` stops holding the whole file several times over** (#805). The write streams group-at-a-time through the new `laterite-ags4-emit::MatrixStream` door (`write_ags4_matrix` is now a loop over it — one serializer, and a differential test pins the bytes) straight into a temp file beside the destination, renamed over it only on success — so the #423 refusal still leaves an existing file untouched, now test-pinned on both doors. Append mode and a non-UTF-8 `encoding=` take the byte-building door, which returns `bytes` across the PyO3 boundary instead of a `str` the caller immediately re-encoded. Output bytes are unchanged — the python-ags4 parity oracle holds by identity. `laterite-ags4-emit` 0.14.0 (the additive door), `laterite-ags4-merge` 0.12.1 rides the moved floor (coherence gate).

**The shipped pyarrow-free pandas hop registers the native table straight into DuckDB** (#834, memory-queue M5). `compat.AGS4_to_dataframe`'s DuckDB fallback — the hop a default `pip install laterite[compat]` takes — copied every group's Arrow table into polars purely to rename positional columns before registering it into the engine. The copy is gone: the native table's own Arrow capsule registers directly and the rename rides the SQL projection (quoted identifiers with embedded quotes doubled, source names taken from the engine's own view of the registration, and the column-count-mismatch ValueError kept by the same strict zip). Output contract unchanged — frames byte-identical across typed/ragged/hostile-heading/empty groups, and the python-ags4 parity oracle holds by identity on BOTH hops (pyarrow present, and import-blocked to force the shipped one). What the paired re-measure actually found is on the ticket and the campaign ledger: the intermediate was never the shipped hop's big memory premium — that survives the fix, unattributed, in the DuckDB bridge leg itself — so this lands as a modest read win for the shipped install shape, and the owner's dep-shape evidence trigger fired.

**Breaking: the parse leaf's cells are spans over one retained decoded buffer.** (#838, queue M4; shape: `dec-parse-cell-representation`). `laterite-ags4-parse` used to own every cell as its own `String` — one heap block per cell, under every read-shaped operation on every surface — and the validating profile re-owned every full line on top. Now `ParsedFile::text` retains the whole file's decoded text once (`Arc<String>`, adopted zero-copy — the `Arc<str>` form the design page sketched was measured putting a whole-file transient copy exactly at the operation peak), `RawLine.text` and `DataRow.values` are `u32` spans into it, and a cell whose source carried `""` escapes is unescaped once at parse into a fix-up region of the same buffer, so every read stays a plain `&str` through the unchanged `cell()`/`col()` accessors. The tokenizer's state machine moved to `split_ags_line_spans` and `split_ags_line` became its adapter — one machine, agreement by construction (`scan_line` could not serve: it genuinely disagrees with the tolerant reader on a mid-field quote). The `retain_raw_lines` knob is gone — a retained line costs ~a span, so the profile split collapsed to decode policy plus the explicit opt-ins — and `ParseError` gained `TooLarge`, refusing a >4 GiB decoded text instead of silently truncating an offset. Measured on the campaign's committed instrument (fresh-child peak RSS, A/B/A-bracketed, A-legs within 0.05%): validate −29.0%/−36.5% of peak and read-typed −28.4%/−35.5% at the 25/100 MB rungs, with criterion `parse_bytes` 43–47% faster and the rules-only pass inside the noise floor; the full record is on the ticket and the ledger's M4 row. Breaking for `ParsedFile` consumers (parse, validator re-exports, core at minimum); python-ags4 parity held by identity and every surface's read contract is byte-identical.

fixed.text: **A fractional value under a 0DP heading now rounds on emit, like every other DP width.** It truncated toward zero — `212.9` kPa declared 0DP was written `212`, understating by up to one unit of the declared precision, always downward, so every ratio derived from the file leaned one way. No sibling behaved like this: 1DP-and-up already round half-even, and python-ags4 formats 0DP with the same rounding, so the fix removes a parity divergence as well as the bias. What a 0DP cell *accepts* on read is unchanged — this is only what emit writes for an in-range fractional value.

added.text: **Rule 10c now names the link it cannot check.** The rule asks one question per group — does this row's copy of the DECLARED parent's KEY tuple exist in that parent? — and a KEY heading owned by some other group is not in that tuple, so the link it stands for is never asked about: a file can reference a row that does not exist through such a heading and validate clean. Neither engine is wrong. python-ags4 asks the identical single-parent question and agrees on every arm of the demonstration, and AGS4 gives a GROUP one `DICT_PGRP`, so the second link is one the FORMAT cannot express. `lat validate --show-fyi` now says so, as `FYI (Related to Rule 10c)`, naming the group whose link goes unchecked. It does not say the declared parent is the wrong one — sometimes both links are real and AGS4 can only carry one, which is the finding rather than a defect in the file. It is advisory and moves no verdict, because it cannot be anything else: **the shipped dictionary contains the shape** — `LBST` declares `LBSG` while keying on the whole `SAMP` tuple in every edition, and `PMTL` declared `PMTG` while keying on `PMTD_SEQ` in 4.0.4 and 4.1, having declared `PMTD` in 4.0.3 and lost the heading again in 4.1.1. **The containment test is the check, not a refinement of it**: a group is a candidate parent only where the child's KEY tuple contains that group's WHOLE tuple, and `DISC` is the counter-example that forces it — it keys on `FRAC_SET` without FRAC's `FRAC_FROM`/`FRAC_TO`, so FRAC was never a candidate and DISC stays silent. Two classes are dropped and the code says which: the parentless groups, where 10c checks no link at all, so an advisory naming one of them would imply the rest were checked; and a heading whose four-letter prefix names no group — the specimen headings are KEY across the whole lab-test family and no SPEC group has ever existed, which without the filter would hang a permanent advisory about an absent parent on every one of them. A candidate that is an ancestor of another candidate goes too, so LBST's unchecked SAMP link is reported once rather than once per generation. Reported from an AGS-L layer where the same shape lets a triaxial test number orphan silently (#759).

**The DuckDB extension's behaviour is now checked, not just its documentation.** The nightly duckdb leg verified that the published extension installs and that every documented SQL example runs — and nothing else. An extension that installed cleanly, ran every example, and returned different rows from `lat` on the same file passed the entire job, which is how the DuckDB surface became the least-observed one we ship. **The checker for this already existed here and had never once run.** `laterite-ags4-compliance`'s `duckdb-parse-check` asks whether the extension's `read_ags()` produces the same content-addressed key set (`_id`/`_parent_id`) as the core reader every other surface wraps — those keys are golden-tested byte-identical across surfaces and carry no float or temporal formatting to drift between a SQL result and a Rust reference, so *same keys* is exactly *same rows*. What was missing was its INPUT: the producer that asks duckdb the question lived only in the dev satellite, so the comparator in this repo had nothing to read and was never wired to anything. A checker with no input is indistinguishable from no checker, and nothing said so. `tools/compliance/emit_duckdb.py` supplies that input here, and installs the extension from the DuckDB community repository — the artefact a user actually gets, rather than one built beside the checkout, since a local build can agree with the engine while the published one does not. First run: 635 of 635 registry groups agreeing across 83 fixtures on extension v0.10.0, with the 13 non-standard groups it cannot key-check reported rather than left implied. Two stale comments are corrected alongside it, both of which had been read as reasons this could not be done here: `laterite-ags4-xcheck`'s manifest called the parity oracle **private** when `PyOracle` is public in this workspace, and the checker's own header said the whole harness lived in the satellite when only its producer did. The fixture corpus is python-ags4's own public test suite, and its version is derived from the declared dev dependency rather than restated — two hand-written copies of that pin already exist with a gate that knows about exactly those two, and a third would have sat outside it (#719).

**One command cuts every surface at one number, and a nightly report says when one is owed.** The `product` and `engine` version tiers were split in 2026-08-01 for a good reason — a browser-only patch used to bump every surface — but the split left two bumps that are two decisions, and the second one is easy not to make. It wasn't made: the product shipped three times while the engine stood still, so crates.io consumers, and `laterite-duckdb` which pins the engine crates from the registry, sat four figures of public API behind what every wheel user was running. `tools/release/cut-release.sh <version>` stamps both tiers in one `release: X` commit and prints the publish sequence in dependency order, because the order is forced: engine to crates.io first, then the product tags, then the DuckDB extension, which cannot move until the crates are on the index — and whose caret requirement means it will not pick a new minor up on its own. `--skip engine` is the escape hatch and exists for exactly one case: crates.io is append-only, so burning eleven crate versions on a browser-only fix is a cost worth being able to decline. The two numbers stay two fields for the same reason — they are defaulted to the same value, not merged, because collapsing them would spend that option permanently. `tools/release/release_status.py` derives the part rather than asking you to remember it: the engine verdict from the committed `cargo-public-api` snapshots, which are the only source that can see an addition (`cargo semver-checks` has no `function_added` lint at all, and skips every minor lint between releases); the product verdict from the changelog sections every PR already has to fill in. It prints what it cannot see on every run — the product's own API surface is unmeasured, and neither tier is checked against a registry, so a stamped version whose tag was never cut stays invisible. It runs nightly into the step summary, and cannot fail: unreleased work is a state to decide about, not a defect, and a nag that can go red gets silenced. Running the cutter for real immediately found a release blocker that reading could not: the wasm README's usage example prints the version, making it a version stamp in all but name, and it was never added to the bump list — so the next product release would have failed its own `test_shipped_readmes_carry_no_superseded_version` check. That is the second instance of a class the release script already documents, and it now stamps (#716).

**`forge describe` can draw organic ground and peat, behind a flag.** The BS 5930 description engine covered the two natural inorganic lanes, so a synthetic borehole log could never show organic soil or PEAT — ground that is unremarkable in the field and, being described by a different set of terms, exactly the sort of text worth putting in front of a validator. `describe --organic` opens a third lane: Table 20's *slightly/very organic* qualifiers ride as ordinary secondaries so the standard word order still holds, and PEAT becomes a principal in its own right, led by Table 21 condition rather than by consistency or relative density, typed by clause 33.4.6 (fibrous / pseudo-fibrous / amorphous), and coloured from its own hue set because the general palette is inorganic-plausible and reads wrong on peat. The von Post humification scale is deliberately absent — the standard does not use it for field description, and a scale reading would be a fabricated measurement rather than a generated description. `--principal <SOIL>` and `--lane <coarse|fine|peat>` filter the drawn pool instead of steering the draw, so `--seed` keeps its meaning and each row still reports the seed that produced it. **The lane is opt-in for a reason that outlives it**: the draw is one shared random sequence, so a third branch shifts every subsequent draw and every seed yields a different file — which re-bases the benches drawn from this engine AND a downstream consumer's committed output, in their repo, on their schedule. Nothing failed when that happened, because the determinism contract only asserts that a seed reproduces itself. It fails now: the default draw is pinned to bytes captured before the lane existed, so a re-roll has to be argued past a red test. The pin says the draw moved; it cannot say a consumer was told, and the design page records that half as an obligation rather than a gate (#697).

**A divergence declared reader-facing is now reader-facing at the rule too.** Two bodies of divergence prose disagreed about who hears what, and nothing said whether that was deliberate: a practitioner who tripped the rules behind an unrecognised or blank `TRAN_AGS` got an explanation on the docs page and in the demo, and silence from the webapp's rule explainer — the one surface reached by hitting the rule. The rule is now stated and gated: a record the canon marks `user_facing` must be cited by at least one rule in the catalogue. It runs ONE WAY on purpose — a note on a record that is not `user_facing` is not a fault, because the catalogue speaks to someone looking at a failing file and plenty of internal divergences belong there without earning a reader-facing summary, which is most of the citations that already existed. What it forecloses is the quiet direction, where adding `user_facing` to a record ships it to the docs site and leaves the rule silent. Seven records earned notes, each attached to the rule its own canon body names rather than to one guessed from its title. `tools/check_rule_catalogue_refs.py` carries the check beside the identity one it already ran, with its own failure banner, because the shape is the opposite — a record with no citation, not a citation with no record — and the fix is to write the note rather than repoint one. Two limits are printed on every run rather than left to a green tick: the membership check inherits the existing blind spot exactly, so it can say a record is cited SOMEWHERE and never that it is cited on the right rule; and the demo's third body is deliberately outside the rule, since it is generated from the states the demo can reach and gated by the parity workflow, which makes its membership a measurement rather than a decision (#683, #640).

**Every state the landing demo can reach is now swept through BOTH engines, and the answer is checked in.** The demo tells a reader that laterite and python-ags4 answer differently in places, and that claim was being made from a handful of hand-checked states. `tools/gen_demo_state_map.py` enumerates the reachable states, emits each through the demo's OWN emitter (loaded through Vite, not reimplemented, so every state is provably reachable rather than merely plausible), dual-validates each with forge, and writes `web/landing/demo/state-map.json` — both engines' rule keys and per-rule counts per state, with python-ags4's version recorded beside them because the map is a claim about a specific version. `--check` is a drift gate in `parity.yml`, so a validator change that moves a demo state cannot land silently. Every difference is triaged to a documented record; an unrecognised one FAILS the run rather than being written down, because it is either a new O-N or a defect in one of the two engines. The sweep is exhaustive to one lever from the seed and says so on every run — the product of the levers is exponential in the group and row counts, and cell values are unbounded so they are covered by equivalence class (#659).

**`forge edit` — structured edits to an AGS4 file that already exists.** Set or blank a cell, add or delete a row, drop a column or a whole group, several at once from a `--patch` file (`--patch-template` prints a worked one). Every line no operation names is written back byte-verbatim, each keeping its own terminator, so the difference between input and output IS the edit and a no-op is provably a no-op; a line that IS named is rebuilt canonically through the repo's own field quoter, because splicing a value containing a comma into a field that was not quoted would tear the row. Rows are 1-indexed over the ORIGINAL data rows, so a patch reads the way it was written however much it changes, and operations apply in a canonical order rather than the order they were listed — asking to delete a group and also to edit a row in it can only mean the delete. A group, row or heading that is not there is refused by name before anything is written, as are the two shapes that cannot be edited coherently: a file declaring one GROUP code twice, and a row too short to carry a column being dropped. Nothing is written at all without `--out` or `--in-place`: the default run is the preview, and its report carries `unchanged`, which is the no-op property made observable. It exists because hand-manipulating AGS text produced three wrong results in a row during the Rule 10c investigation (#655).

**The docs' js examples are now type-checked against the shipped `.d.ts`, not just executed.** The page-program runner's bar is "does not raise", which cannot see an example running the wrong branch — the recorded case branched on `report.ok`, a field `Report` does not have, so the expression was always `undefined` and the page demonstrated the opposite of what its prose claimed while passing. `tools/check_doc_types.py` runs `tsc` (resolution-only: a name or signature that no longer exists fails; an example's loose style does not) over the assembled page programs and the node/wasm example files, against `laterite`'s `dist/index.d.ts` and the wasm package's generated types. Every run starts with a positive control carrying exactly that defect, which must go red before the corpus is believed green; an unbuilt leg is reported by name, and the two known checker-limit suppressions are printed and stale-checked on every run (#565).

**A “Coming from python-ags4” page** — the drop-in had no front door. `cookbook/compat.md` is task-shaped (“how do I do X with the shim”); this is arrival-shaped (“I have python-ags4 code and I am deciding”), and the two want different readers and different lifetimes. It carries the one-token claim and why it is structural rather than approximate, the module map with `ags4_cli` named as a deliberate non-mirror, the permanent non-goal of a top-level `python_ags4` import name (it would collide in `site-packages`, and as a separate distribution it would break this repo's own parity oracle), how to read the upstream pin off `compat.PYTHON_AGS4_COMPAT`, and the exit-code answer a migrant actually arrives with. That last one is the #321 half: through `compat.check_file` nothing changes shape because it runs the FYI tier and not the warning tier, and on the native surface a warning is shown without failing the run. The gap list itself is not copied — `compat-surface-gaps.json` is the authority and a copy would be quietly wrong one upstream release later.

**Two harnesses that measure what a certificate is worth on the validate path.** #271 asks whether the free `validate()` on Python and Node should gain the `index=` parameter `read()` already has, and made the answer conditional on a number nobody had: how much of a validate run is parse rather than rules. `tools/bench-cert-parse-share.py` measures it through the CLI — the one shipped surface that already has the door the proposal would add, so it stands in for the parameter without anyone building it first — and `tools/bench-cert-python-routes.py` measures the three Python routes in-process, including the handle route (`read(index=).validate()`) that decides the question, because the proposal's incremental win is only what the handle route still pays. Both report the instrument's own resolution rather than a bare figure: min, median and spread over N repeats, and the baseline run twice, at the start and the end, with the run refusing to report a split if the two disagree by more than a tenth. The CLI harness measures its process floor explicitly instead of assuming it away, because folding startup into a parse share makes parsing look cheaper than it is, which biases the answer toward not building — the error worth being loud about. Fixtures come from `forge scale`, so they are reproducible from a seed and carry no real delivery data. Neither harness fires a heavy CI job; they are the first tools added since `code` stopped listing `tools/**`, and `test_paths_filter` now pins that.

**`validate()` takes a certificate on Python and Node — the verdict without the parse.** `read(index=…)` could hand a cert to a handle, and a handle parses by definition, so the cheapest question a certificate can answer — *is this file still error-clean?* — was the one neither surface could ask. The engine has always been able to answer it from the bytes' hash and the stamp without parsing at all; the CLI reached that path through `--index` and the Rust facade through its own free `validate`, while Python and Node could not, because the only door they had built a handle first. Both now take `index=` / `{index}` on the free `validate` as well, and the register records it as a change of FORM rather than a new capability — cert-input was already `present` on both. The two doors are not two spellings of one thing and the docs say so: `validate(index=)` skips the parse and leaves you nothing to query, `read(index=).validate()` parses to build the handle and skips only the rules. Measured before it was built, per the issue's own condition (#497): parsing is about half a validate run, and the new door is ~10x faster than the best route that existed. **Naming a cert is an assertion**, so a stale one raises `StaleCertError` from either door, and raises BEFORE the rule engine — a mismatch reported afterwards would cost exactly what naming a cert is meant to save, which is why the freshness check moved into the binding rather than being copied into the wrapper where it would have read the file a second time. A cert merely INHERITED by `Ags4File.validate()` still falls back with `revalidate_reason`: nothing was asserted at that call, and turning an existing chainable verb into a raising one is not a bug fix. Autodiscovery is still refused on both surfaces — a sibling `<file>.ags.idx` does nothing unless you name it.

**The landing demo edits like a spreadsheet where you have a mouse, and keeps the row carousel where you have a thumb.** The split reads the pointer, not the width — a phone in landscape is still a touch device. On a fine pointer a click selects the cell, a second click or Enter opens the value in place, arrows move the selection, typing replaces, Tab commits and moves on, Esc restores; every commit revalidates live, exactly as the carousel always has. Both editors gain **row delete** — a per-row ✕ on the table and a button in the carousel — so the Rule 13 teach-loop (add a second PROJ row, watch it flagged) can be unwound without resetting the whole demo. And the delivery being one immutable value made **undo/redo** cheap: Ctrl/Cmd+Z walks back cell edits, row adds and deletes, applied fixes, even a reset — with Shift, forward again. Two new Playwright lanes pin the split: a coarse-pointer project proves the carousel still opens, pages and closes, and the fine-pointer lanes drive the keyboard surface — selection, in-place editing, undo.

**One finding vocabulary across the landing demo.** Findings rendered three hand-rolled ways depending on where the engine attached them — red boxes in the prose column for group findings, differently-red boxes under the carousel's field card, severity boxes in the panel — and the reader had to learn each one meant the same thing. One shared callout now carries them all, its tint mapped from the engine's own severity (an unknown tier renders as an error on purpose — loud, not unstyled). Cell-level findings wear the same grammar in the cell itself: severity tint replacing the key tint, the marker in the severity's colour, and a tooltip carrying the rule and the engine's description. Group-level findings move out of the essay and onto the table they judge. And panel rows gain a group chip — colourless, because band colour means group identity and never severity — which is what finally tells apart the two Rule 16 findings the engine correctly reports with byte-identical text against SAMP and LLPL.

**TRAN joins the landing demo as an editable cover sheet, and Rule 14 stops being a life sentence.** The seeded delivery had no TRAN group, so “TRAN group not found” was a permanent finding no demo interaction could clear — the page's reach-green story dead-ended on it. The seed now opens with a clean transmission header — who produced the file, for whom, against which AGS edition, its headings drawn from the generated dictionary schema like every other table — rendered in the File section as an ordinary editable group table with the same modality split, finding grammar and undo as the four above (the strata ramp stays at seven; a cover sheet is about the file, not a stratum). Rule 14 now fires only when the reader deletes TRAN's one row — a finding they can cause, read in the cover sheet's own strip, and unwind — and blanking a required value raises Rule 10b live. The Python gate pinning the seeded finding set moved in the same change, as did every narration that counted or named the retired finding.

**A Rule 10c parentage check that is DECLINED now says so.** A child row whose parent key fields are all empty claims no parent, so the link requirement does not apply to it (O-39) — and until now that row simply produced no finding, which is exactly what a row that passed the check produces. A deliberately standalone record (a lab control, an off-site sample) and a key blanked or typo'd by accident were indistinguishable from the report. Such a row now carries `Warning (Related to Rule 10c)` naming the parent group and the key fields that could not be checked. The verdict is unmoved — a standalone row is still not an orphan, warnings never decide a verdict, and `--no-warnings` suppresses the tier as before. It is shown by default on `lat validate`, the wasm surface and `laterite.validate()`; `laterite.compat` does not carry it, because that surface is python-ags4's shape and python-ags4 has no equivalent. Recorded as O-52, which also corrects O-39: python-ags4 does not skip these rows deliberately. Its `rule_10c` has no skip at all — the rows go unreported because its tables include the UNIT/TYPE pseudo-rows on both sides of that merge, and the parent's UNIT row has empty key cells, so an all-empty child key matches it. Give that UNIT row a value under a key column, which is legal, and python-ags4 reports the child's own UNIT row as an orphan.

**O-53 — a blank `TRAN_AGS` is reported once, and the schema it fell back to is stated on the verdict rather than on the cell.** Neither validator can resolve an edition from a blank, so both fall back (O-30) and judge the file against a schema its author never declared. Both say so, in different places. python-ags4 stacks its unrecognised-edition FYI onto the cell, on top of the Rule 10b error that blank already earns, and because the FYI tier is opt-in a default python run reports the blank but never says which schema it then used. laterite returns early on an empty value — the unrecognised-edition finding is reserved for a value that is present but unknown (O-45) — and carries the fallback on the report envelope instead, as `Report.dict_version` and `Report.resolution`, which `lat validate` renders on its first line as `dictionary 4.1.1 (fallback)` against a resolved file's `dictionary 4.1 (exact)`. Unconditional, at every tier, once for the file rather than once per offending cell. The record exists because a difference that is invisible to the parity gate (an `FYI` key is not an `AGS Format Rule N` key) was also invisible to the demo state map until both engines were compared unfiltered.

**The landing demo now explains a divergence where the reader meets it, instead of asserting one in prose.** The page has always claimed laterite and python-ags4 answer differently in places; nothing on it said WHERE, or let you reach one. Editing a cell into a state the sweep found now surfaces the explanation beside the finding it is about, drawn from the committed state map and never computed: `tools/gen_demo_state_map.py` writes a second, small `web/landing/demo/divergence-notes.json` beside the map (the map itself is evidence, and two orders of magnitude too large to ship to a landing page), and a difference shape with no note FAILS the run — a difference the demo says nothing about is indistinguishable, on the page, from a state that has nothing to explain. The two directions are matched differently, deliberately. Where laterite reports something python-ags4 does not (or both do at different tiers) the note keys off the RULE KEY, so it hangs on the finding already on screen and generalises to states the sweep never enumerated. Where python-ags4 reports something laterite does not there is no finding of ours to annotate — that IS the case — so it renders as its own panel, keyed to the cell the state was reached by against the literal value the enumerator wrote. Deciding *is this value non-ASCII for its declared type* in the browser would have put a second validator on the page to disagree with the first. The panel is kept apart from the findings by three carriers besides colour: a dashed border where every callout's is solid, a heading naming the other tool and its version rather than a rule, and no click-to-focus (a finding jumps the file pane to its line; this has no line). It is not counted in the scoreboard, and on the desktop side it sits inside the findings scroller so it costs the panel no height. Pinned in the landing lanes by O-N identity rather than by count, at both the narrow and wide viewports (#660). The third case the ticket named — the same rule raised by both engines at different counts — gets a refusal rather than a render path: it is not a difference shape, no O-N covers one, and none has ever occurred, so a generic path for it would be code on the page that has never rendered. The generator STOPS if one appears, which is the stronger half of not-dropped-silently. Both that guard and the no-note-for-a-shape guard are unreachable from a live sweep, so they are pinned directly in `tests/test_demo_state_map_guards.py` with a positive control beside them.

**The landing demo shows what python-ags4 actually reported about the delivery on screen, beside what laterite says.** It said the two engines differ in places and then showed one number, leaving a reader to guess what the other tool made of the same file. The header now reads laterite's count and python-ags4's, with the release the second number is a claim about — and the number is **read, never computed**: python-ags4 is a dev-only dependency and does not run in a browser. It comes from the swept state map, keyed on laterite's own finding signature, which is the rule-key-to-count map the demo already has from its own run. That key is legitimate because the sweep measured it to be: the swept states collapse to far fewer signatures than states and python's answer is constant across all but one of them. **The exception is resolved rather than smoothed over** — clearing `PROJ_ID` or any of several `TRAN` cells leaves laterite saying exactly the same thing, and only a blank `TRAN_AGS` earns python's extra FYI (O-53) — and it resolves on the same one-cell string comparison the existing divergence panels use, because the alternative is a second validator in the page disagreeing with the first. A signature the sweep never measured **says so**, because silence is indistinguishable from the two engines agreeing, which is the confusion this whole line of work exists to remove. Three refusals keep it honest, none of them reachable from a live run and all of them pinned by tests: a SECOND collision that no single cell can tell apart fails the generator rather than reaching the page; a collision whose discriminating cell the majority also holds fails the same way; and a swept state raising a laterite **FYI** fails outright, because the sweep measures both engines with every tier on while the demo's own validate call takes the wasm default of FYI off — the same number only while nothing raises one, which was true by accident and checked by nothing. The sweep also gains a sixth value class. The five it had are each engineered to reach a named rule and none of them is the thing a reader actually does, which is type a phrase into a cell; the new one is ordinary prose, applied to the four surfaces where free text can change an answer (KEY columns, typed columns, PA columns, and any column at all if the text is non-ASCII). The columns where it is inert are **named** rather than enumerated, with the reason, because an unstated exclusion reads as a surface that was swept. How many states the sweep reached and how many columns it declared inert are printed on every run and carried in the map, where `gen_demo_state_map.py --check` fails if the committed answer has moved (#673).

**`forge edit --set-unit` — rewrite the UNIT a heading declares.** `edit` could change values but never the declarations above them, so a heading's units were whatever the synthesizer chose — and Rule 15, which asks that every unit used be listed in the UNIT group, had no injector at all, because nothing could put a unit into a file that the UNIT group did not already define. `--set-unit LOCA:LOCA_GL=mAOD` does, and a file built that way trips Rule 15 on both engines. Only the locator is split on `:`, so the unit itself may carry them — which matters because AGS date-time headings declare units full of colons, and those are exactly the ones this reaches for. An empty value leaves the UNIT present but undefined; worth knowing that on its own that is NOT a Rule 15 violation, since both engines skip an empty unit, so a file that only empties one dual-validates clean. A group carrying no UNIT row is refused by name rather than having one invented beneath it.

**`forge edit --set-type` — declare a heading's TYPE and re-format the column to satisfy it.** The scaffolds emit a handful of the AGS types, and a heading's type was whatever they chose, so a question like *do the two engines agree on a `3SF` column?* had no file to ask it with. `--set-type LOCA:LOCA_GL=3SF` projects an existing column into any type the AGS type system can read; `--set-type-raw` moves the declaration and leaves every value alone, which is how a cell that contradicts its own type gets made on purpose. A `DT` column is rendered at the precision its UNIT declares — including a UNIT set in the same patch — rather than at whatever the value happened to carry. Values that cannot satisfy the new type are refused by group, heading and row rather than mangled, and nothing is written when one is: half a projected column is worse than none of one. Note that re-formatting alone does not leave a spec-valid file — a type code absent from the file's TYPE group is a Rule 17 finding — so a clean projection is `--set-type` plus an `add-row` into TYPE, which one `--patch` does in a single pass.

**`forge edit --add-column` — give a group a heading it does not have.** It lands in every descriptor row the group carries and as an empty cell in every data row, so the arity stays consistent and nothing trips on a ragged row. Cells start empty on purpose: the caller decides what goes in them. A heading the group already has is refused — a locator that meant two columns is the ambiguity this layer refuses everywhere else — but a heading the dictionary has never heard of is accepted, because manufacturing that is the tool's job and judging heading names is the validator's. Combined with `--set-unit` and `--set-type` in one `--patch`, this creates a column, declares it and fills it in a single pass, in whatever order the operations were listed. Note that an added column left undeclared is not neutral: its empty TYPE cell is a Rule 17 finding on python-ags4 and not on laterite, which is the divergence O-19 already records — declare the column's TYPE and both engines return no findings at all.

**`forge edit --insert-row` — put a data row at a position, not only at the end.** A fault could previously be planted only in a row that already existed or in an appended one, so "what happens when this row is in the middle of the group?" was not a question the tool could ask. Positions count the file's original data rows, the way every other locator here does, so an insertion does not renumber the rows a later operation names, and two insertions at one position keep the order they were listed in. A position past the last row is refused rather than quietly appended — appending is what `--add-row` is for, and a typo that silently becomes an append gives a reproducer that does not reproduce. A row inserted at position 1 lands under whichever descriptor rows the group actually carries, which matters for the malformed files forge makes on purpose.

**`lat merge --tran-description` and `--tran-remarks`, on all three launchers.** `lat` could state the five REQUIRED TRAN headings and had no way to state the two OTHER ones, so a merged file stamped from the shell could not carry a description or a remark at all. The flags land on the native binary, the wheel's console script and the Node launcher together, because the guide describing them is one document mirrored into all three packages — two of those copies would otherwise have documented flags their program rejects. While in that block: the help for `--tran-producer`/`--tran-recipient`/`--tran-status` called them *optional*, which was true of an older issue-plus-date rule and has not been since all five became required together, and `--tran-issue` still said it worked "with --tran-date" alone.

**Breaking: `on_missing_tran` — merge can be asked to refuse an unstamped merge rather than warn.** Merging two valid deliveries without a transmission stamp produces a file that fails its own validation: each delivery carries its own `TRAN`, `TRAN_ISNO` is a KEY heading so the two issue numbers do not collide, both rows survive, and Rule 14 allows exactly one. The caller was warned and had no way to ask to be stopped — which sat oddly against the rest of merge, where a TYPE clash refuses by default, a UNIT conflict is fatal in every mode, and a half-stated transmission stamp is unconstructible rather than left for a rule to report afterwards. `on_missing_tran="error"` makes the same refusal available one level up, before any bytes are emitted; `"reconcile"` is the default and is exactly today's behaviour, so nothing existing changes meaning. It is read only when no stamp is supplied. Available as `on_missing_tran=` (Python), `onMissingTran` (Node and the browser), `Merge::on_missing_tran` (Rust), and `--on-missing-tran` on all three `lat` launchers, whose accepted values are projected from the engine's own enum rather than retyped. The refusal is a merge refusal like the two beside it: the same exit code, its own `missing_tran` token so a caller can tell which of the three it hit. Breaking for the engine crates only, and only for a direct Rust caller: `MergeOpts` gains a public field and `MergeError` a variant, neither of which an existing struct literal or exhaustive `match` survives. Every laterite surface is source-compatible — the option defaults to today's behaviour on all of them.

**The modality register's grid is now held whole, not just well-formed.** Every guard over the cross-surface register read the cells that existed: `test_register_well_formed` iterates the cells a capability declares, and `gen_modality.py --check` compares the rendered page to the JSON, where a missing cell renders faithfully as nothing — so both agreed while both omitted the same row. Twelve capability x surface pairs held no verdict at all, ten of them on the CLI. All twelve are now recorded: five CLI absences that rest on the surface's file-tool promise, `emit` x CLI which does not (emit is a component there, not a user-facing verb), `diff` x DuckDB (an output-shape decision, not the read-only manifest), four python-only views absent on their siblings, and `transport-pack` x browser as a P3 gap — the browser already loads zstd and runs it inside `lock`, so the zstd-only door is wiring rather than new capability. The new assertion reads the generator's own `uncovered()` predicate rather than restating it, so the count printed on every run and the pair that fails CI cannot drift apart.

changed.text: **The generated crate pages stop restating the version.** Thirty of the thirty-five files an engine bump touched existed to say the same number again — 20 wiki crate cards and 10 shipped READMEs, both rendered by `tools/gen_crate_graph.py`. Not a drift bug: they are generated, so they cannot go stale, and both spellings qualified the number as the workspace's. The cost was review surface, on every breaking PR, for a line one field of `Cargo.toml` already holds. **The README half was also the wrong number to give a reader**: `Currently v0.11.0` sat directly under `cargo add laterite-ags4-core`, which resolves 0.9.0, because the tree runs ahead of the registry for most of a cycle. That is only wrong in the repo — a published README ships alongside the version it names, so the crates.io page was always self-consistent — but the repo is public and the README is the crate's front door in both places. What is rendered now is the version TIER, which is a fact about the scheme rather than a reading: *the engine crates move in lockstep on the workspace version*, or for the facade, *this crate versions independently of the engine*. The unpinned `cargo add` already answers *which version*, and is the only thing that can answer it correctly. `_version_of` is replaced by `_inherits_workspace_version`, so the number is no longer computed where it should not be rendered. The faithfulness test that asserted both renderings stated the SAME version is re-aimed rather than deleted — that disagreement is now structurally impossible, so it checks the two facts still rendered — and a new one asserts no generated block carries a version at all, since re-adding one would be invisible except as diff weight (#783).

**The semver gate compares against the release, not against `main`.** A version number is a promise to whoever ran `cargo add`, so the baseline has to be what they got. `check_semver.py` carried its own switch-over condition — *"at the point where every publishable crate has a release the registry baseline should replace this"* — and all eleven now have one. The git baseline had a defect that read as strictness: both sides of the comparison carry the SAME version, so `cargo semver-checks` inferred `no change; assume minor` and failed every break, including one the tree's version already accounted for. That is why three breaking PRs in three days each took their own bump (#730 → 0.10.0, #741 → 0.11.0, #776 → 0.12.0) while the registry served 0.9.0 throughout — a gate demanding numbers nobody could install. **The replacement is narrower and says so on every run.** Once the tree is ahead of the registry semver already permits the change, so cargo skips every lint; that is the correct answer and it means the gate enforces nothing for the rest of a cycle. Rather than report green over an empty run, it prints each crate as `ENFORCING` (level with the registry, every lint live) or `ahead` (the version pair already permits it), with the counts left to cargo's own per-crate line rather than recomputed. The window it does gate — right after a publish — is the only one in which a missing bump could reach a consumer. `--baseline-rev` survives as a hand tool for the different question it was answering. The partition is unit-tested across all three states after a first draft passed with the `absent` branch deleted, which is the shape of test this gate's reporting contract cannot afford (#782).

**`lat --readme` follows the house punctuation, and the page that renders it is gated rather than excused.** The docs-site em dash policy had one page permanently outside it: `reference/cli/` IS the shipped guide, `include_str!`d into the binary and read from inside the wheel, so rewriting it changes what a program prints rather than what a site says. That made it a decision rather than an edit, and the decision is that the policy covers terminal output too. Three prose sentences in the authority (`rust-packages/laterite-cli/README-cli.md`) are rewritten as sentences rather than character-swapped, and the two generated mirrors follow. The `lat --help` blocks are untouched: they reproduce what the tool prints, and the gate skips them as code wherever they appear. Removing the exclusion also closes a blind spot the exclusion had created, and one nothing else could have caught: the note `web/docs-site/scripts/gen_cli.py` writes above the guide is ours, and it has no `.md` for the source half to read, so while the page was skipped by path nothing held that note at all. The gate's own test for the exclusion is replaced rather than deleted, by the thing it stood in for — a dash in that page's prose now has to make the gate red, which an exclusion re-added under a differently-spelled prefix could not satisfy (#681, #588).

**`lat validate` now states which dictionary judged the file — on every launcher.** The head line gains `— dictionary 4.1.1 (exact)` on the native binary and the wheel launcher; the npx launcher already said it, which under the launcher contract's fact tier made its absence elsewhere a defect, not a style choice. The `exact`/`guessed`/`fallback`/`forced` token is the same resolution vocabulary the certificate and the `report.resolution` API already use (#542).

**`npx laterite diff` states the whole delta, not the abridged one.** Its human output gains the `a → b` header, the heading-only groups its `added || removed || changed` filter used to drop, the `groups added:` / `groups removed:` lines and the `total:` line — the same facts the other two launchers state, in this launcher's own layout. The new human-content gate (`tools/xcheck/check_cli_content.py`, nightly) compares those facts across all three launchers and reports any launcher it could not run (#542).

**Breaking: a warning no longer fails a validation run.** The severity tiers decided what a report *showed* and what it *concluded* with one dial, so a file whose only blemish was an unrecognised `TRAN_AGS` edition — no rule broken — exited `1` and failed a CI job. Errors decide the verdict now; warnings stay visible by default and are reported, not fatal. Opt back in with `--warnings-as-errors` (CLI), `warnings_as_errors=True` (Python), `warningsAsErrors: true` (Node, wasm) — the compiler's `-Werror`, opt-in for the same reason. `--no-warnings` is unchanged and still controls what you *see*; passing it together with `--warnings-as-errors` is now rejected rather than silently resolved. `Report.is_valid` follows the verdict instead of `count == 0`, so a passing file can carry findings, and new `errors`/`warnings`/`fyi` counts expose the split. Every surface reads one `Verdict` in the validator rather than keeping its own copy of the formula, so `is_valid` and the exit code cannot disagree.

**A custom dictionary that overrides a standard heading's type or status is now an FYI, not a warning.** #321 gave the warning tier a rule — a warning predicts a downstream *surprise*, where a consumer silently receives something other than the author meant — and this is the one site out of seven that fails it: the caller declared the override in the dictionary they passed, it is honoured exactly as declared, and nothing downstream differs from what the file says. Re-parenting a standard group and demoting a standard KEY both stay WARNINGs, because both change row identity and the rules that key off parentage and KEYs then answer differently about rows nobody edited. The demoted finding moves to its own `FYI (Related to DICT)` label, leaving `DICT` warning-pure — the separation `Warning (Related to Rule 18)` already exists for, and the reason `compat`'s `count_errors` can classify it at all (a bare `DICT` key matched none of its branches and counted as nothing). See O-51.

**Reader-facing prose across the app, landing, and docs drops the clean-room licensing rationale** — the app shell's footer credit, the landing footer, and seven docs pages said the validator is a clean-room implementation and that this is what permits the MIT licence. Readers need what the tool does for them, not why its licence was possible, so each location keeps only what serves the reader — at most the fact the aside was carrying: the engine is one independent implementation of the published AGS4 rules, results can differ from python-ags4's, and COMPAT.md / OBSERVATIONS.md record where and why. No behaviour changes; wording only.

Sharing one renderer was weighed and ruled out: `comfy-table` lives in `laterite-cliutil`, which is bin-side because the validator library's lean dep-graph is a hard guarantee, so the only way to make `npx` draw the same box is a third hand-written implementation.
