Its handful are known-unfixed rather than absent, and want their own ticket. Every sentence was rewritten rather than repunctuated: a dash standing in for a reason became one, an aside became brackets or its own sentence, and a correction became a full stop and a short follow-up, which usually lands harder than the dash did. The generated page went back to its generator, not to the rendered file: `reference/divergences.md` is rendered from `observations.json`, so its share was fixed in the records' own `user_facing.summary` fields and in the generator's page header, and the gate names that on a failure rather than inviting a hand-edit the next regeneration undoes. Both halves print their scope on every run, pass or fail, and not only when unhappy: fenced blocks and inline code in the source, `<pre>` and `<code>` in the built pages, are skipped and COUNTED, because an output capture that prints an em dash prints it because the tool did, and rewriting one would make the page a claim about output nobody can reproduce. The stylesheets and the two scripts are counted for the same reason, so "out of scope" is a number a reader can see rather than an assumption (#588).

**`forge edit --patch-template` now prints a worked projection.** The example was a cell edit and an appended row — two unrelated operations that showed the file format and nothing else. It now shows the thing the command is for: create a column, declare its UNIT and TYPE, put a value in it, and add the type code to the file's TYPE group, which together give a file that dual-validates with no findings on either engine. The header states the canonical order, so a reader learns that listing order does not decide the result before they discover it by accident.

**`build_ags4`'s emit adds nothing to its peak memory any more.** The validating re-parse never needed validate-during-emit — it needed sequencing: the formatted copy now drops before validation, which puts the re-parse entirely off-peak with the validator untouched, and the PyO3 host consumes its input row by row within a group through a new consuming entry point, `emit_ags4_owned(Vec<GroupInput>)` (#789). Row-by-row matters when one group dominates — per-group consumption still holds a 2.4M-row group's whole input live as its last row formats. After this and the `EmitGroup.rows` fix (#788), the high-water mark is set by the caller's input finishing, before formatting starts: 27.1x the emitted output down to 10.7x, requested bytes at peak, on the workload recorded in the issues. `emit_ags4(&[GroupInput])` is unchanged for every existing caller.

**The engine crates version per-crate — the lockstep is retired.** Ten crates.io crates shared one number inherited from the workspace, so one crate's breaking change stamped and published all ten, a browser-only fix once burned a version on every surface, and an unchanged crate's version history said nothing. Each published crate now carries its own version (the `laterite` facade's own line was the precedent), moves when it changes, and publishes individually — heterogeneous numbers across the set are the design, not drift. For a crates.io consumer nothing moves until the next per-crate bumps land; from then on `cargo add` sees versions that mean something happened in that crate. The release tooling followed: `bump_crate.py` bumps one crate (its manifest and its `[workspace.dependencies]` floor together), `cut-release.sh` cuts the product alone, and the nightly release-status report derives a verdict per crate from its own API snapshot.

deprecated.text: **`laterite_ags4_validator::is_valid` is renamed `is_clean`; the old name is deprecated, not removed.** The free function returns `true` when a run produced zero findings — the same answer as the verdict right up until the entry above changed that. Two public `is_valid` in one crate, disagreeing on a warning-carrying file, is a trap set for whoever reaches for the obvious name next, so the one that does not mean the verdict gives the name up. `is_clean` is the house phrase for what it computes: every surface's report already prints `clean (0 findings)`. Same signature, same polarity. The old name stays as a `#[deprecated]` delegating alias — a crates.io consumer should meet this as a warning naming BOTH replacements, since the two now answer different questions and they have to choose, and a hard break would give them nothing to choose from. It is inventoried in the reliquary for deletion in the release that bumps the engine tier.

fixed.text: **Breaking: a DATA row with more fields than headings is refused, not quietly shortened.** A file that used to read now raises on every read surface, which is the point — it was reading back wrong. Rows bind to headings by position, and the surplus bound to nothing — so the read dropped it and handed back a row that looks complete. The usual cause is AGS4 Rule 5: a value containing a comma whose quotes were lost, where `Acme, Bloggs and Co` arrives as two fields and NOTHING can say which side of the comma the heading wanted. **Everything downstream then agreed the file was fine**, which is what made this worth a refusal rather than a warning: the shortened row still satisfies Rule 4, so it validates clean, `certify` mints an `.ags.idx` asserting errors *measured, count 0*, and a re-emit writes the truncated value back out fully quoted — a file that is now conforming AGS4 and no longer says what its author wrote. `lat fix` was never a way out either; it declines Rule 5 as ambiguous, correctly. The reader now refuses, naming the group, the line and both counts, as `DuplicateHeadings::Error` already does for the sibling failure one axis over — there a name collided, here a position has no name. **Only the direction that loses something is fatal**: a SHORT row still pads to `""`, because the missing tail is knowable and nothing is discarded. `ExcessFields::Truncate` (`--truncate-excess-fields`, `truncate_excess_fields=`) opts back into the old behaviour for salvaging a file that cannot be repaired at source, and its own documentation says the result must not be round-tripped or certified. The blast radius is the read codec, so `lat read`, the Excel export and the read handles move; `lat validate`, `fix`, `diff` and `merge` parse through the validator and are untouched — the repair path stays open on exactly the files this now refuses to read. The sliced read reaches the same verdict, restating the slice's line number in whole-file terms rather than naming a plausible line 3 of a group that starts at line 4000 (#776).

**The rules-catalogue drift gate was watching the copy, not the source.** `web/public/rules-catalogue.json` is a verbatim copy of `rust-packages/laterite-ags4-reference/data/rules_meta.json`, and `src/lib/rulesCatalogue.test.ts` holds them byte-identical — a real gate, in the required `unit` job. Its trigger was the `web:` paths filter, which watched `web/**`: the copy, never the source. So #770 (Rule 10c's O-56 note) and #774 (Rule 14's `mixed` severity) each edited the source, tripped no `web/**` path, never ran the gate, and merged green over a drift that was already real. It surfaced days later on two unrelated PRs that happened to wake the job for their own reasons, which is the worst way to learn it — the red lands on whoever is passing, not on whoever changed it. The copy is re-synced, and the filter now names the source file, because **a gate whose trigger does not include the thing it compares against fires everywhere except where the change was**. The gate itself needed no change; it was correct and unreachable.

**The rule catalogue no longer says Rule 14 is error-only when it can hand you a warning.** `lat rules` reported `severity: "error"` for Rule 14, while a default `lat validate` could emit `Warning (Related to Rule 14)` — a `TRAN_AGS` that is present but not a recognised edition satisfies the rule and still earns a warning, because the file was judged against a fallback dictionary its author never declared. Rule 14 is now `"mixed"`, matching Rules 1, 10c, 16 and 18, and its description names the warning the way Rule 18's already did. The record was contradicting itself: O-45 has described that warning all along. The gate that should have caught it compares two hand-written lists to each other, so a rule missing from both sides was invisible to it; Rule 14 has been added to the emitter list as well. `lat rules --json` output changes for this one rule.

**A date-only `DT` cell survives a `read()` → `build_ags4()` round trip without needing a fix.** An AGS4 `DT` column declares its precision in its UNIT — 40 of the dictionary's DT headings say `yyyy-mm-dd`, 41 say otherwise — and Rule 8 judges the cell against it. A typed datetime carries no such precision: `read()` deliberately promotes a date-only cell to midnight, and the Arrow transpose then rendered that as `2021-08-09T00:00:00`, which fails the `yyyy-mm-dd` unit the heading itself declares. A clean file read back and re-emitted came out dirty: `strict` raised, `report` reported, and only `autofix` was clean — by repairing what we had just mis-written. Typed temporal columns are now rendered at the precision their heading declares, on all three surfaces (Python, Node, wasm). **The declared precision decides, not the value's own zeros**, which is what keeps the fix from trading one broken round trip for another: the same midnight instant stays `2021-08-09T00:00:00` under a heading that declares seconds, because truncating there would break a file that is clean today. A render that would LOSE information — a real time under a date-only unit — is refused outright, so a genuine mismatch between the data and its heading still reaches the caller as a Rule 8 finding instead of being silently trimmed. The same rule fixes the reverse direction nobody had reported: a date-only value under a heading declaring time is padded rather than left failing. It is applied in the Arrow transpose, not in the emitter's cell formatter, and that placement is the load-bearing part: the formatter emits strings verbatim so the validity MODE owns canonicalisation, and a caller's own string stays the caller's. A typed temporal column has no caller-authored string to preserve, so its spelling was always ours — which is why this is the layer that can act without spending that contract. The design page had named a `truncate_dt_to_unit` helper as doing this job for six weeks after it was deleted as dead code, which is how the defect came to be reported against behaviour the documentation said was already handled. The capability is back as `dt_to_unit_precision`, not as a revert: the original sliced by byte offset, so a non-ASCII DT cell panicked, and having no caller, nothing ever found that. The replacement validates the cell's shape before it indexes and declines anything malformed (#695).

**`forge seed-vendor --dry-run` no longer clones over the network and writes the corpus.** It was the only subcommand that reached the network and the only one whose `--dry-run` did nothing: the context arrived unbound, so nothing it did could consult the flag. The agent-first CLI contract states the guarantee flatly — `--dry-run` mutates nothing — and the subcommand where a mistaken probe costs a network round trip and a directory of files is exactly the one worth probing. The check now lands before the clone rather than before the copy, and reports both sources, since a real run falls back from GitLab to the GitHub mirror and a plan naming only the first would misreport what it may do (#708).

**`forge gen --help` lists every injector the binary accepts, not seven of the ten.** `rule10b`, `rule14`, `rule16` and `rule17` parsed fine and appeared nowhere in the help, so a caller who read it first — which is what help is for — never learned they existed. The list is now rendered from the same catalogue `forge catalog` reads, so the two cannot drift; aliases and the scaffold-qualified form are named rather than enumerated, the qualified suffix being open-ended. A hand-maintained list in a doc comment is what produced the gap (#709).

**`forge edit --patch-template` runs without a `<FILE>`.** It prints a static template and reads no file, but the argument was required, so the obvious invocation failed with an error implying the template is per-file. It is a discovery flag — it exists so a caller can see the patch shape *before* they have a file to apply one to — and demanding the file inverted that. The requirement is lifted for that flag alone; every mode that reads a file still demands one (#710).

**The demo's verdict chip rides the masthead instead of parking over the page.** It was `fixed right-4 bottom-4` — a clickable overlay on top of whatever the page happened to have in its bottom-right corner, which for this demo is tables. Walking the page and hit-testing under it found a fix button at one desktop width, a cell editor at another, and three separate controls on a phone; the only clean width was the one where the content column stopped short of the corner, which was luck rather than design. The e2e suite could not see any of it and still cannot on its own: Playwright scrolls a target into view before clicking, which lands it clear of a viewport-fixed chip, so the scoreboard test clicked the very button the chip covered and passed throughout. From the breakpoint the text nav uses, the chip now sits in the sticky masthead — no overlap, still a door to the findings panel, still following the reader. Below it the chip stays the corner float: the phone masthead has single-figure free pixels against a chip that needs eighty-odd, and the 390 touch reader was recorded as this chip's audience when it was built, so hiding it there is a design decision this did not carry. That leaves the phone case KNOWN rather than fixed, and the landing lane pins it as a state rather than skipping it, so whoever solves it is told by a red test. Two mounts rather than one, because a single mount in the header rendered as a corner float on phones traded the overlap for a focus order that no longer matched what the reader saw; each size now gets the mount that belongs where it draws, sharing one on-screen signal so they cannot disagree. The regression test measures CONTAINMENT — the chip's box inside the masthead's — after a first attempt that walked the page in viewport steps passed against the unfixed code, because a sampling walk steps over a collision and at that lane's viewport height its stops landed either side of all three (#691).

**The carousel's page dots are a small mark inside a full-size target.** The dot WAS the button, at ten CSS pixels in a six-pixel gap, which misses 2.5.8 twice over: the target is under the 24-pixel minimum, and because it is undersized it does not reach the spacing exception either — a circle of the minimum diameter centred on each dot intersected its neighbours. The mark keeps its diameter and the button grows around it to the full target size. That necessarily widens the row, since targets that do not overlap sit a full target apart on centre where these sat closer, and the extra air is the visible cost of the fix: overlapping the targets instead would have held the old spacing and satisfied a checker that measures elements one at a time, while the covered strip went to whichever painted last and the dot underneath went back under the minimum for the half a reader aims at, with nothing red anywhere. The landing lane pins the hit box by MEASURING it — each target's rendered box, the absence of encroachment between neighbours, and the mark still being small — rather than asserting that a utility class changed, so a rename cannot satisfy it and a restyle cannot quietly shrink it back (#679).

**The call to action clears the AA text bar, and rust stops being a text colour.** `--cta` had been held to the 3:1 floor a UI component answers to, which is the wrong bar for a filled button: its label is text, so 1.4.3 applies and the resting fill was under it. Raising the fill was blocked in both directions at once — `--fg-on-cta` is already all but white, so only the fill could move, and darkening it made rust worse everywhere rust carried TEXT. So rust was retired from that job: the "runs something" button keeps its rust wash and rust edge and takes a maroon label, which is the call the outline CTA had already made on "maroon reads, rust acts". The obvious replacement fill — one step down the brand ramp — turned out to collide with `--warn` under simulated colour-blindness, below the floor `separation.test.ts` holds, so an action and a warning would have read as one colour for exactly the readers that gate exists for. Sweeping the whole 8-bit space against every gate at once returns plenty of colours that pass and NOT ONE ramp step among them, so `--cta` is now a literal, written the same in both themes — which makes the identical-across-themes property explicit rather than emergent from two ramps happening to offset by one, a property that had already failed once (#403). `--chart-1` moves with it, as the separation gate requires, and the docs' generated token bundle is regenerated in step. The contrast gate's CTA floor moves 3:1 to 4.5 so the old bar cannot come back, and it now records what it CANNOT see: it compares token pairs, so an opacity modifier is invisible to it — which is how two faded labels sat under the bar with the gate green (#682, #680, #406).

**Links that sit inside a sentence are underlined at rest, and the demo's controls say what they act on.** Colour alone was carrying "this is a link" in the footer, the install prose and the demo's explanatory text (1.4.1); standalone card doors keep their bare treatment, because a card is already shaped like a door. The table's accessible names now lead with the cell's value rather than trailing it, so "Label in Name" (2.5.3) holds for the readers who speak the visible text at a control — that alone took the landing from thirty-seven failing elements to one, and the one left is a bare glyph toggle the checker exempts. The table's sub-label moves from `--fg-faint` to `--fg-muted`: the token itself could not be raised, because to clear the bar it would need the value `--fg-muted` already has, leaving the ramp with two identical steps (#682, #680).

**The demo's UNIT, TYPE and ABBR groups now carry the standard descriptions.** Eleven were the demo's own wording rather than the AGS4 dictionary's: `m` as "metres" not "metre", `PA` as "Abbreviation list" not "Text listed in ABBR Group", `CP` as "Cable percussion borehole" not "Cable percussion (shell and auger)", and so on. Teaching material a reader may copy should be the real thing. Only the ABBR drift was checked — that is the O-43 FYI — so UNIT and TYPE had no gate at all and nothing would have caught them. The reader sees no change: the demo validates with the FYI tier off, so the two flagged ABBR descriptions were never shown, and the seed's four visible findings are the same four. What changes is the divergence map, and substantially: that FYI was the ONLY difference in 145 of the 150 swept states, so the demo's claim to differ from python-ags4 almost everywhere was an artifact of two typos in our own fixture. It now differs in 5 states, which are the real ones (#659).

**Dropping two columns from one group with `forge edit` now removes both.** Each removal shortened the line the other was indexing into, so the second one took the wrong field or ran off the end — which surfaced as a spurious "row too short" refusal or, for a row the same patch had appended, a silently ragged row. Which of the two happened depended on the order the flags were written in. Columns are now resolved against the original headings and removed right-to-left, so the pair means the same thing either way. Found by a `cargo mutants` sweep: the surviving mutant was on the bounds guard that was absorbing the fault (#655).

**The minimizer no longer tears a value that contains a comma.** Its field pass split a DATA line on `,` with no quote awareness, so shrinking a value like `"north, then east"` dropped ` then east"` — cutting the value in half and leaving the quote unterminated, at the SAME field count, so no arity rule noticed. When the input already violated Rule 5 the tear added no new finding either, so the signature held and the shrink was accepted: the reproducer that came out was not a smaller version of its input but a differently-broken file. It now reduces through the same tokenizer-backed layer as `forge edit` (#655).

**A landing-demo cell write that could not land still cost the reader an undo step.** The demo's store decides whether to record history by IDENTITY — a mutation that hands back the delivery it was given records nothing — and every mutation but the cell write upheld that explicitly: the row delete bounds-checks its group and row index, the row add resolves its group, the group delete and restore test membership. The cell write compared only the cell VALUE, so for a group that is not present, or a row or column index outside the row, it compared a string against `undefined`, never matched, and rebuilt an array whose contents were identical to the original. No write outcome changed then and none changes now — that rebuild matched no cell either — but the reader was charged an undo step for a write that did nothing, and the Ctrl/Cmd+Z that followed appeared to do nothing at all. Reachable rather than theoretical: the selected-cell paste resolves the clipboard asynchronously and commits against an index captured at keydown, so pasting and then deleting that row lands a commit on a row that is gone (that capture is its own defect, #580, and this does not fix it — a merely reindexed row is still in range). The column bound is the target ROW's own length rather than the group's heading count: a DATA row shorter than its HEADING row is a real AGS4 shape, and this write has never extended one (#581).

**A newline pasted into the landing demo's table silently truncated a row, and the damage landed on a group the reader never touched.** The fine-pointer table's selected-cell paste is the one entry path a browser does not sanitize for us: every other way a value reaches a cell — the in-place editor, the carousel's field cards — is a single-line `<input>`, while the handler read the clipboard itself and committed the string as it came. One terminator in a cell is enough to tear a DATA record in two, because the demo's emitter doubles an embedded quote and escapes nothing else, so the byte reaches the emitted text raw. The demo's own parser — narrow on purpose, it reads the one fixture the page ships — then splits on it, and the fragment after the break opens with no data descriptor, so the tag chain DROPS it rather than reading it as a record: the row count survives and every column past the break vanishes, which is why a rows-length assertion would have passed straight over this. The lossy path is reachable, because applying one group's fixes reparses the whole file and the fixer is scoped by group — so pasting into one table and clicking Fix on another destroyed a row nobody was looking at. The engine was never at fault and is untouched: it keeps an embedded terminator as field content, flags it under Rule 6, and already ships the repair. The handler now applies the rule a single-line input applies, and the model's `setCell` applies the same rule on the value, so the editing path cannot seat a terminator in a cell whichever caller reaches it. (`emit` and the parser are unchanged and still assume clean cells, so this closes the reachable route rather than making the invariant structural.) That rule is taken from the BROWSER rather than the spec — an interior break becomes a SPACE, not nothing; a CRLF pair counts as one break; and a TRAILING RUN of breaks, however many, is dropped entirely — because reading HTML's value sanitization algorithm suggests stripping every break and a live paste says otherwise on both counts. The e2e measures the answer off a real input and compares the handler against that measurement rather than against a second copy of the same literal, which is what catches a normalization rule that is merely self-consistent.

**`npx laterite fix` prints its result to stdout** — the applied/residual line went to stderr via the launcher's `note()`, so `npx laterite fix delivery.ags | …` saw nothing while the native binary and the wheel's `lat` printed theirs to stdout. The agent-first contract routes resolved-mode results to stdout; this was the one stream divergence among the three launchers. The result line also gains the distinct fix kinds (`[reformat_numeric]`) the other two launchers already state — the new content gate caught the omission — and pins both (#542).

**`lat diff --json` and `lat merge --json` no longer escape non-ASCII on the uvx launcher** — the wheel's `_cli` re-serialised the diff delta through `json.loads` → `json.dumps` (whose `ensure_ascii` default turns `boué` into `bou\u00e9`) and did the same to the merge summary's out path, so the same command printed different bytes depending on the launcher. `diff --json` now prints the engine's own render verbatim on all three launchers — one shared renderer beside the `RevisionDelta` type — and the merge audit arrays serialise off the engine structs, with two non-ASCII xcheck cases pinning both documents byte-identical (#542).

**`lat --readme` was a different document depending on how you installed it, and `lat <verb> --help` worked on one launcher of three.** `surfaces/cli.md` opens with "It is the same tool however you launch it"; the guide each launcher prints is part of that claim and it was not true. The wheel ships its own copy of `README-cli.md` — `_print_readme()` reads it from the installed package — and every gate reads the Rust crate's copy instead, so nothing compared them. The wheel's had last been touched by a bulk tree sync in July while the authority moved on: it documented `--check-files` under `## certify`, which is the EXACT line `tests/test_cli_readme_flags.py` exists to prevent and which `CertifyArgs` has never had; it did not mention `--warnings-as-errors` at all, so `pip install laterite` shipped a reference predating the verdict split; and its exit-code prose described an engine that had stopped behaving that way. A gate that can only see one of two copies guards a file, not the claim. `tools/gen_cli_readme.py` now generates every mirror from the one authority and `tests/test_cli_readme_mirrors.py` holds them byte-identical, which is what makes the flags gate's reach real — everything it proves about the authority is now true of every launcher rather than of one file. **Verb-scoped `--help` came with it**, because the guide's own Usage block promises `lat <command> --help` and only the native binary delivered it: the Python launcher tested `"--help" in argv` position-blind across the whole of argv, so `lat certify --help` took the same branch as `lat --help` and printed all 203 lines — the document the reader reached for `--help` to avoid — and the Node launcher had no help path at all, so the flag fell through to the unknown-flag refusal and exited 5 while shipping the document that told a reader to use it. Both now slice the verb's own `## <verb>` section, plus `## Global options` because clap lists those under every verb too. **No launcher writes help prose**: a fourth description of the same flags is the class of defect this fixes, one level up. The lookup matches a verb against the WORDS of a heading rather than its first token, because `## transport — pack / unpack / lock / unlock` documents four verbs at once and a first-token rule drops all four back to the whole guide — silently, which is the shape of the original bug. The npm package ships the guide for the first time; `pack-smoke.mjs` fails a tarball that drops it, since that is a break only an installer would ever see.

**The `node` job never re-ran its own docs-output gate when the generator changed, and a stdlib-only script bought a full build.** One path filter, wrong in both directions at once. `ci.yml`'s `code` filter listed `tools/**` — along with `ags-wiki/.bootstrap/**/*.py` and `examples/**/*.py` — for a single reason the comment above them stated plainly: `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` were steps in the `python` job, so every linted file had to fire that job or go unlinted. Lint has since moved to the unconditional `repo-gates`, and the globs outlived the reason for them while still charging for it: `code` gates seven jobs, so editing a release helper that imports nothing but the standard library bought a cargo build, the PyO3 cdylib, the pytest suite and a post-install wheel smoke, to validate a script whose actual gate had already run. `code` now enumerates the nine tools a gated job runs, plus the two a test opens. In the other direction — and this is the half that was silently broken rather than merely wasteful — the `node` job runs `gen_doc_outputs.py --check --surface node` and nothing in the `node` filter named the generator, so an edit to it re-ran the PYTHON surface's drift gate and not the node one. That is #207's shape exactly, live, found by the check that replaced the old one rather than by reading the list. The check that held `tools/**` in place asked the question through ruff (“is this file linted”), which stopped being the right instrument the day lint moved; it now derives from `ci.yml`'s own `run:` blocks and requires every gated job's filters to reach every tool that job invokes, so a future narrowing fails here instead of disarming a gate.

**Seven numbers this repo now owns were reserved as another repo's.** The bare-`#N` gate added last week freezes a set of numbers known to belong to the private satellite, so they cannot be written bare again. #473, #475, #488, #492, #493, #494 and #495 have since been issued HERE, which is the collision the gate was built to describe arriving at the gate itself: a bare `#495` now correctly means this repo, and the frozen set would have failed it for being a number that used to mean something else. Those seven are released — every existing citation of them is already qualified, and the gate only ever matched bare numbers, so nothing loses cover. The rule is recorded where the data lives: an entry leaves the set the day this repo's numbering reaches it, so the set shrinks over time and what remains is exactly what a bare reference cannot yet legitimately mean. The falsifiability test picked its exemplar by literal and asserted that #475 was still reserved; it now takes the lowest number the set still holds, which is the one nearest to being claimed next.

**`--no-warnings` did not suppress the custom-dictionary override warnings.** `emit_override_warnings` took no `CheckOptions` and ran unconditionally, so a flag whose entire contract is "errors only" left three findings on screen — and the engine's own tests asserted them under `CheckOptions::default()`, which is errors-only, so the missing gate looked exactly like a passing one. Reachable from every surface that accepts a custom dictionary. It mattered more the moment one of those findings became an FYI: the FYI tier is opt-in, and an FYI nobody can turn off is not one.

**A validator test claimed to cover the type-override branch and never reached it.** `override_warnings_flag_reparent_demotion_and_type_change` described `SAMP_TOP` as "a standard non-KEY heading" being retyped and asserted only that some finding mentioned it. `SAMP_TOP` is `2DP/KEY` in the base, so it is a second KEY demotion and the assertion was passing on the demotion message. The branch was covered elsewhere, on `LOCA`, which is why nothing looked wrong — but a fixture that cannot reach the code its name claims is worth no confidence at all.

**The Validate and Fix panes told you to try again, next to no Try again button.** Both share the tier-1 engine channel and deliberately have no retry control — the channel retires a dead worker, so the next file, paste or sample starts a fresh one — yet a failed engine download ended “Check your connection and try again.” on all four surfaces that render one. That names an affordance only Explore and the Excel converter have, and it is the same inherited-affordance fault the shared copy already fixed one branch over, on the crash line. The two tier-1 panes now close on “Load your file again to retry.”, which is the recovery they actually offer. Explore and the converter are unchanged.

**An aggregated bar chart drew its folded tail as several bars stacked at one category.** The colour-by caps how many values keep a palette slot and folds the rest into one neutral “Other” (#445). For a point cloud that fold is a POOLING of points, which is exactly right — there is nothing to merge. On a bar with an aggregate the query had already grouped by (category, colour), so the tail arrived as one point per folded value per category and ECharts drew them at the same place, at the same width, one over another: a single visible bar with nothing saying more than one value was underneath it. The merge was never available where the fold happened — the right one is the aggregate's own, and `avg` has none that is honest, since a mean of means is not the mean without each group's row count, which the plotted rows do not carry. So that path now folds in SQL, inside the `GROUP BY`, where the aggregate runs over the merged group's raw rows and `avg` is as correct as `sum`, `min` and `max`. Three costs are deliberate rather than overlooked: the plot query is composed only once the ranking probe has answered, so it is no longer a pure function of the form controls and its round trip is serialised behind the probe's; the SQL disclosure pane shows the folded query, which is the one that ran; and on that path both queries render the colour as text, because a `CASE` naming the fold otherwise resolves to the column's own type in DuckDB and fails the whole query converting 'Other'. Scatter and line compose exactly as before.

**A failed chart query said “No rows to plot for this selection”.** That is an answer — the query ran, the delivery had nothing to show — and it was printed under the red banner reporting that the query had not run at all. It now says which of the two queries failed and that no chart was drawn: the colour ranking is a second query the reader never asked for, and on an aggregated bar its failure stops the plot query being composed at all, so naming the wrong one leaves the reader hunting a fault in a query that never ran.

**The landing page rendered zoomed-out on phones.** Below the 64rem breakpoint the group sections’ grid children kept `min-width: auto`, so the nowrap tables’ min-content sized the page — a 390px phone got a 783px layout viewport scaled down to fit, and every table’s own scroller sat inert because the page had grown instead. The width floor now holds at every width (`min-w-0` on both grid children): the document stays exactly viewport-wide and each table pans inside its own scroller, which is what the table component promises — nine columns on a phone move the table, not the page. A landing lane in the Playwright suite pins the contract at a strict 390px viewport, with no mobile emulation — emulation absorbs exactly this overflow into zoom, which is how it shipped unseen.

**The borehole rail’s scale hid its first tick and disagreed with its own pill.** Three geometry defects, one cause each: the rail inset itself with padding its absolutely-positioned children ignore, so “0.00 m / Surface” rendered under the sticky masthead (visible during macOS overscroll bounce); the pill, probe and veil positioned through an inset run while the bands and ticks used a plain 0–100% run, so the depth the pill showed never matched the tick label beside it; and ticks marked section tops only, so the bottom of the hole went unlabelled. The inner box now insets with offsets, ONE shared mapping positions bands, ticks, veil, probe and pill — unit tests pin that a tick and the pill land identically at the same depth — and a terminal tick labels the seeded final depth, read from the delivery fixture so a LOCA_FDEP edit moves it with no code change. A desktop lane joins the landing Playwright project to hold the scale’s geometry.

**Two rule notes cited a divergence record the catalogue had retired.** The rule catalogue carries practitioner-voiced notes about where laterite differs from python-ags4, rendered beside a rule wherever a reader meets one — and they are a second body of prose beside the OBSERVATIONS canon, with nothing holding the two in agreement. Rule 9's note cited O-10 and Rule 14's cited O-20; both records are marked superseded by O-30, and Rule 9's said so in its own text while still pointing at the dead one. Rule 9 now carries ONE note describing the edition resolution that actually happens (per file, from `TRAN_AGS`, with bare `"4.0"` taking the newest 4.0.x patch, AGS 3.x a hard error, and anything unrecognised falling back to 4.1.1 exactly where python-ags4 does) instead of a fixed default that has not been true for some time, merged with the second O-30 note it had been sitting beside. `tools/check_rule_catalogue_refs.py` is the gate that keeps them true: it fails on a note citing a record that does not exist or one the canon has superseded, checks identity rather than wording (the two bodies of prose are written for different readers and are meant to differ), and states on every run that it cannot check which rule a note hangs off, because the canon does not record that.

**The demo state map compared one engine filtered against the other whole, and every difference it reported in that direction was an artifact.** `tools/gen_demo_state_map.py` dual-validates each enumerated demo state through the forge, whose python side goes via `tools/py_ags4_check_json.py` — a bridge that filters python-ags4's report down to `AGS Format Rule N` keys. That filter is exactly right for the parity gate, whose contract is error-key parity, and exactly wrong for a sweep that also compares the warning and FYI tiers: python-ags4's `FYI` and `General` keys were dropped while laterite's equivalents were kept, so the comparison could only ever find differences pointing one way. It found them. The map's first revision recorded a drifted abbreviation description as a laterite-only finding in nearly every state, when python-ags4 raises the same FYI with the same message; and it recorded the unrecognised-TRAN_AGS shape as one python-ags4 "does not report at all", contradicting O-45's own text, which says python reports it as an FYI. The bridge now takes `LAT_PY_AGS4_ALL_KEYS=1` — an opt-in the sweep uses and the parity gate deliberately does not, so that gate's contract is untouched — and reports on every run, pass or fail, how many keys it dropped and which. `General` is dropped in both modes as report furniture rather than a finding: python-ags4 prints it ahead of the error list, and every site that raises it (the AGS3 caveat, the extended-ASCII note, "could not complete validation") emits prose about the run beside the real finding, never in place of one. With both sides whole the map's difference shapes are tier differences on findings BOTH engines raise, not silences — and one of them had no record, so O-53 now covers it. One more hole closed while fixing it: `parity.yml`'s `demo` path filter listed the generator and the enumerator but not the bridge, so the very edit guaranteed to move every state at once was the one edit that would not have run the drift gate.

**An unstamped merge now says what it actually did to `TRAN`.** Merging without a transmission stamp emits a `tran_not_stamped` warning, and that warning claimed the merged file *"kept the newest input's TRAN as a fallback"* — which reads as one surviving row. It keeps all of them. `TRAN_ISNO` is a `KEY` heading, so reconciliation has a key to work with and simply never sees a collision: two deliveries carry two different transmission numbers and both rows survive, leaving a file that fails Rule 14, which requires exactly one. A caller who read the old wording and moved on shipped an invalid file believing the fallback had handled it. The warning now describes the reconciliation and names the consequence, and the same correction is applied to the Rust, Python, Node and wasm docs and to the merge decision page, all of which restated the old claim. Behaviour is unchanged; whether an unstamped merge should refuse rather than warn is a separate question.

**The Rule 16 explainer described a concatenator default the validator does not apply.** The rule catalogue's own text — what the web app shows beside a failing file, and what `lat rules --json` emits — said multi-abbreviation fields are "split on the TRAN_RCON concatenator (default +)". The specification does name `+` as the default when `TRAN_RCON` is absent, and neither laterite nor python-ags4 applies it: an undeclared concatenator leaves the field unsplit and checked whole, so a file concatenating on `+` without declaring it gets one finding naming an abbreviation it never used, and nothing reports the missing `TRAN_RCON`. A reader looking for why was told the opposite of what happened to them. The explainer now describes the behaviour and carries a note saying what to do about it (declare the separator); the divergence itself is recorded as O-54, unchanged.

**Breaking: `TranStamp.description` and `.remarks` now reach the emitted `TRAN`.** Both fields were accepted and silently dropped — on `merge` and on `build_ags4`, from Python and from the CLI. `remarks` contradicted its own documentation, which promised the value would be appended to merge's provenance note. The engine was never wrong: `synthesise_tran` appends rather than replaces and writes `TRAN_DESC` when one is given. It was unreachable. `TranStamp::from_parts` — the boundary adapter every surface funnels through so that exactly one place decides what counts as a complete stamp — took five parameters and hardcoded the other two to `None`. Node and the browser had worked around it by reapplying the values after the fold, which is why the fault looked surface-specific; they now go through the seam like everyone else. `TRAN_DESC` and `TRAN_REM` are OTHER headings, so they stay outside the all-five-or-none rule: five parts with no description is still a complete stamp, and a description with no transmission behind it is now the same error as any other partial stamp rather than a silent discard. On a merge `remarks` is appended to the provenance note; on a build there is no note to append to, so it is `TRAN_REM` verbatim — a distinction the Python and Node docs now draw. `laterite_ags4_emit::TranStamp::from_parts` goes from five parameters to seven, which is a source break for anyone calling it directly, so the engine crates take 0.10.0. Nothing on the wheel, the npm package or `lat` changes shape — those call the seam, they do not re-implement it.

**The published crates' docs.rs pages stop pointing at things a reader cannot open.** Twelve doc links on public items resolved to private ones — `BaseSpec::Auto` naming `detect_base`, the merge modes naming their lattice helpers, `ags4_codec` naming `from_shared` — and rendered on docs.rs as links that go nowhere. They are plain code spans now: the name still says what it is, without promising a page that cannot exist. Two sample-output blocks (the AGS4 writer's and the codec's) were being parsed as prose rather than code, so their angle-bracket placeholders were swallowed as markup and one line had been garbled by an earlier partial fix; both are fenced now and render as written. Three links in `laterite-ags4-forge` that named real items but did not resolve now do. `cargo doc` runs in CI for the first time with warnings as errors, so none of this can come back unseen.

**`cargo add laterite` no longer resolves two-minors-stale engines.** The facade published at 0.1.2 declares `^0.9.0` floors on its engine crates, and a 0.x caret never crosses a minor — so after the engine tier's 0.11.0 publish, the facade went on handing its consumers 0.9.0 engines, and the publisher's skip-by-version ("already on crates.io") hid it, the version number matching while the manifest content did not. The facade moves to 0.1.3 — a deps-only patch; its own API is unchanged — so its published floors state the engines it is actually built against.

**Breaking: `EmitGroup.rows` borrows the formatted cells, as its doc comment always said it did.** The field was an owned `Vec<Vec<String>>` under a comment saying the struct borrows, so both hosts — the PyO3 orchestrator and laterite-node — deep-copied every formatted cell just to build the write view, and that copy stayed live across the write and the validating re-parse (#788). The field is now `&[Vec<String>]`. Output is byte-identical and nothing changes on the wheel, npm, CLI or wasm surfaces; the break is for a direct Rust consumer of `laterite-ags4-emit` who constructs an `EmitGroup` or names its `rows` field, who now hands the writer a borrow instead of an owned table.

added.text: **`laterite` takes and returns AGS4 as text — `ags4::read_str`, `ags4::validate_str`, `Written::text`.** The facade could only be handed bytes, so a caller holding a `String` — a template, a database column, a literal — had to write `read_bytes(s.as_bytes())`. That worked, which is why it lasted: it is the workaround, not the door, and Python and Node both offer the door. The modality register (added in #241) is what made the absence legible rather than merely true. Text is a distinct source internally, not bytes wearing a hat, so `encoding` cannot reach it: applying a codepage to already-decoded text re-reads UTF-8 as cp1252 and turns `°` into `Â°`, corrupting exactly the cells the option exists to rescue. That is enforced structurally and asserted both ways — the text form is exempt, the bytes form still transcodes. `Written` now holds a `String` with bytes derived, the same way round as Python's `Ags4File`, so `text()` costs nothing; `bytes()` and `into_bytes()` are unchanged. Every case is asserted as EQUAL to the bytes path rather than merely working, because a convenience form that is a second implementation is a second set of bugs.

**`laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` publish to crates.io at 0.9.0.** Both were prepared in full for the first publish and then held back by a single flag, so day one's frozen surface stayed as small as possible. That deferral is spent. They are new crates at the engine's existing number, so nothing moves to admit them: diff lands in publish wave 3, merge in wave 5, and the nine crates already on the registry are skipped rather than republished. What changes is not that the API is frozen — crates.io makes a *version* immutable, not a surface — but that `cargo semver-checks` and the public-API snapshot now police edits to these two. For merge that is the point worth stating: what publishes is `merge_parsed`, whose `&[ParsedFile]` shape is the one laterite#162 endorses, while the typed merge surface #162 warns about is not published and stays free to design. Both crates gained a README, because a published crate without one has a bare crates.io page and that is not recoverable for anyone who already looked.

**`laterite::transport` — the Rust crate can compress and encrypt files.** `pack`/`unpack` (zstd) and `lock`/`unlock` (zstd + an age passphrase), each in a path form and a `_bytes` form that never touches a disk. The odd part is that this was already *linked*: the facade enables `laterite-ags4-core`'s default-on `transport` feature, so every Rust consumer has been carrying age and zstd in their dependency tree while being unable to call a single function through them. It sits at the crate ROOT rather than under `ags4`, because the envelope understands no format — it will compress a JPEG — and the root's rule is that it stays format-neutral. Same shared envelope as every other surface, so a Rust-sealed file opens with `lat unlock`, Python, Node, the browser, and stock `age` given the passphrase. The two password-carrying builders redact in `Debug`: a derived one would put the passphrase into any log line that rendered the builder, which no round-trip test would ever have noticed.

**The Rust crate mints and consumes `.ags.idx` certificates.** `doc.certify().to_path(…)` / `.to_bytes()` mint one over a file that validates clean, and `ags4::validate(…).index(cert)` offers it back so the rule engine does not run. Spelled on **validate** rather than on read, because this crate's validate is a free function with no `Document::validate()` for a read-time cert to reach. A certificate is never auto-discovered — one sitting beside a file is not consent to trust it — and a stale one cannot produce a wrong verdict, only a slower one: the engine reruns and `Report::revalidate_reason()` says why. Minting is over the ORIGINAL source bytes, before any transcode, which is why `Document` now retains them; certifying the decoded form would mint a certificate that never matches its own file, and every ASCII test would still have passed.

**A certificate can also make a Rust read skip the file.** `read(f).index(cert)).only(["LOCA"])` parses that group straight out of the byte range the certificate records and never looks at the rest of the delivery; `Document::sliced()` reports whether it did. This is deliberately NOT what `read(index=)` means on Python and Node — there a certificate parked on the handle lets a later `.validate()` skip the rule engine, which this facade has no `Document::validate()` to do. It declines rather than risks: a stale certificate, a group the index places in two sections (slicing the first would return a strict subset of its rows, silently), or a transcode that moved the offsets all fall back to the whole-file parse, which is always correct. `only()` on its own is still a plain filter.

**The Rust crate repairs and builds — `ags4::fix` and `ags4::build`.** `fix` is the mechanical repair the browser fix UI runs, headless: from a path, bytes or text, applying the safe set (CRLF, BOM, embedded CR, short-row padding, numeric formatting, the `TRAN` delimiter rows) and re-validating its own output, so `Fixed::findings` is what could *not* be put right rather than what was wrong to begin with. It is non-destructive until you name a destination — in place is the source path passed to `to_path`, not a separate flag, because there is nothing a flag would express that the path does not. The repairs that guess intent stay withheld behind `.risky(true)`, and `risky_available` says how many were held back, so a caller can offer that choice instead of having to know the tier exists. `build` is the data door, where `write` is the document one: hand it `GroupData` rows and it produces AGS4, deriving the `UNIT`/`TYPE` catalogues and validating what it wrote. Cells are a first-party `Cell` enum rather than the emit engine's `serde_json::Value`, which is the facade's no-third-party-type rule doing real work here: it is also what preserves the typed formatting Python and Node get from an Arrow frame, so a number goes through its heading's declared AGS TYPE (`12.5` under `2DP` is written `12.50`) while a string is written verbatim. A row whose length does not match its headings is refused by name — the safe fix set pads short rows, so without that check a miscounted column would come back as a finding about the output instead of as the caller's mistake. Both doors share one call into the emit engine with `write` rather than a second copy of it.

**The Rust crate compares and reconciles deliveries — `ags4::diff` and `ags4::merge`.** `diff` answers what changed between two submissions in *AGS terms*, not text terms: rows are matched by their group's dictionary KEY headings rather than by line order, so a re-sorted borehole list pairs each row with its own prior self, and cells are compared through their declared TYPE, so `1.0` → `1.00` is not a change. A line diff gets both wrong. `merge` reconciles N deliveries in order — a later file wins — with the same KEY-aware row identity, so a re-sorted delivery merges onto its prior self instead of doubling it, and every revision it makes is reported so the merge stays auditable. A column two producers typed differently is **refused by default**: resolving that is a judgement about their data, and `on_type_clash` offers the two honest answers — widen to free text (bytes untouched, type discarded) or promote to the greatest `nDP` precision (never the lowest, which would round data away). A column they gave different *units* is refused in every mode, because no resolution exists that does not silently mislabel one file's values. Those two failures now have their own `ErrorKind`s — `TypeConflict` and `UnitConflict`, carrying the same `type_conflict` / `unit_conflict` tokens the Python, Node and `lat` surfaces already use — rather than collapsing onto one, because they need different fixes. Both doors take a path, bytes, or a read handle; the handle form uses each document **as it stands, edits included**, since diffing the file it was read from would quietly ignore the edit.

**`tests/test_docs_snippets.py` — the docs' hand-written Python is executed now.** `test_docs_examples.py` and `gen_doc_outputs.py --check` both key off the `--8<--` include, which covers 38 of the site's 60 Python fences; the other 22 are literal fragments, and together with `README.md`, the PyPI landing page and `COMPAT.md` nothing ran them (`--check-pages` inspects only *output* blocks, so a literal code fence is not even counted). The new gate treats a page as one program in document order — replaying includes so a fragment inherits the `ags`/`fixed` its page established — executes 85% of literal statements against the installed wheel and resolves names plus call keywords for the rest, with a coverage floor so it cannot decay into name-checking. It runs from a temp dir: these snippets write.

**A docs Python example runs on its own — `uv run ex01_read_typed.py`, no clone.** Prototyped on one example ahead of the other 17. A PEP 723 `# /// script` header pins `requires-python` and an exact `laterite==`, and a fixture arm fetches `examples/sample_site.ags` when the repo-relative path is absent, so the code on the page stays the code you would type in a checkout instead of becoming an absolute path. **Every docs Python example now runs on its own — `uv run exNN_*.py`, no clone.** The prototype is rolled out to all 18 plus the marimo tour: a PEP 723 header pinning `requires-python` and an exact `laterite==`, a fixture arm fetching `examples/sample_site.ags` when the repo-relative path is absent, and a `--8<-- [start:code]` marker so the rendered page is byte-identical to before (asserted for all 18 against `git show HEAD:`). A uniform bare pin makes both die under `uv run` on `ModuleNotFoundError: pandas`, verified. The README gains `uvx --from laterite lat validate delivery.ags` — a zero-install trial.

**A nightly leg asks the reader's question: does the live docs site work against the wheel you can actually install?** Every existing docs gate runs against the working-tree cdylib, so all of them answer "is the site consistent with HEAD" — and the reader is not on HEAD, they are on `pip install laterite`. `docs-vs-released-wheel` installs the published wheel (unpinned, whatever PyPI resolves that day) and runs the examples plus `tests/test_docs_snippets.py` against it, printing the released version beside the tree's. The two steps are calibrated differently on purpose: an example that fails to RUN fails the job, because a reader following the site would get a traceback; a committed `.out` that no longer byte-matches is reported and not fatal, because output drift is the ordinary consequence of the tree being ahead. It stays out of `notify`'s `needs` for the same reason — the docs track HEAD by decision, so documenting unreleased API is a chosen state, and filing an issue about a chosen state is noise that gets muted.

**Seven ungated output blocks are now generated, not hand-written.** `--check-pages` counts `text` fences no example backs; that count was 8 and is now 1. Four new CLI examples (clean-file `--json`, a one-value typo, and the warning/errors-only tier pair, the last three minting their input from the fixture with `sed` so CRLF survives) and two new Python examples close `learn/install.md`, `concepts/severity-tiers.md` and `concepts/one-engine-many-doors.md`. The remaining orphan is `chaining/index.md`'s ASCII flow diagram — a drawing, not the output of anything, so it stays unwired by design: the target is zero GATEABLE orphans, not zero orphans.

**Every crate README example is now a doctest.** Three lines per crate — `#[cfg(doctest)] #[doc = include_str!("../README.md")] mod readme_doctests {}` — point rustdoc at the README, so `cargo test --workspace` compiles all ten (eight execute; two touch the filesystem and are `no_run`). **The Node docs' hand-typed JavaScript is executed now.** `docs-examples.test.ts` and `gen_doc_outputs --surface node` both key off the `--8<--` include, covering 18 fences; 11 more are typed straight into the Markdown and the npm landing page carries 4 — the page a reader sees before `npm install` — and none of it ran. `laterite-node/test/docs-snippets.test.ts` welds each page into one ESM program (imports unioned per module, re-declarations turned into assignment, since ESM forbids the rebind Python allows) and executes it from a temp cwd with the fixture copied in. All four pages run; a fence that genuinely cannot — the wasm type declarations, the `{ arrow: true }` call that downloads a DuckDB community extension at run time — carries a `doc-snippet: skip` marker with its reason.

**`laterite-node/test/peer-range.test.ts` — the published peer range must admit the version we develop against.** Offline and registry-free: if the range you tell users to install disagrees with the version your own tests run against, it cannot be right. That single assertion would have caught the ETARGET above the day it was introduced.

**`docs-vs-released-npm` — the Node twin of the released-wheel nightly.** Installs `laterite` from npm unpinned, then the optional peer exactly as the docs and the runtime error tell a reader to, then runs the docs examples against it. Same calibration as the wheel leg: an example that fails to RUN fails the job, an `.out` byte-mismatch is reported and not fatal, and it stays out of `notify`'s `needs`. Building this job is what surfaced the unsatisfiable `peerDependencies` range, so it had earned its keep before running once — and it will be red until that fix ships, which is the correct signal rather than a defect in the job.

**`laterite.compat` mirrors python-ags4's module layout — `compat.AGS4`, `compat.check`, `compat.utils`, `compat.data`.** The drop-in was one flat module where upstream is a package, so `from python_ags4.AGS4 import AGS4Error` — third-party production code, not a hypothetical — had no laterite equivalent at all. The parity oracle could never have caught this: its shim aliases four distinct upstream modules to one object, so 121/131 green was a statement about flattened function behaviour and structurally blind to module boundaries. Every import shape a real python-ags4 user writes now ports by changing one token, `python_ags4` -> `laterite.compat`, and `tests/test_compat_import_shapes.py` holds that true by asserting placement rather than mere presence — a name drifting between submodules fails even though the flat namespace would still resolve it. The flat namespace is unchanged and remains the primary surface; the submodules re-export from it. `compat.check` also gains `STANDARD_DICT_FILES` and `LATEST_DICT_VERSION`, mirrored verbatim — the fallback is 4.1.1 rather than the newest key, because upstream ships a 4.2 dictionary and still defaults to 4.1.1 when TRAN_AGS is absent — and `compat.data` ships a sample file whose contents are clean-room (upstream's is LGPL-3.0). There is still no top-level `python_ags4` import name in the wheel, now stated as a permanent non-goal rather than an unrecorded gap: two distributions cannot both own `site-packages/python_ags4/`. Undocumented private helpers (`compat._try_dict_version` and friends) moved to `compat._impl` with the body.

**ARM64 Linux is a shipped target again — `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`.** It joins `napi.targets`, the wheel matrix and the binaries matrix, so all three artifacts ship the same platform list. Its 2025 removal rested on a billing dependency on a then-private repo, and on a comment blaming a self-hosted pool `release.yml` never used; neither holds now and the runner is free. Platform parity keeps it honest: a triple shipped by one artifact is shipped by all.

**The shared design-system primitives, in Solid, with a vendored icon set.** Thirteen components both the browser app and laterite.dev import from one place — button, chip, status badge, count bubble, icon, input, select, checkbox, field, dialog, toast, tooltip, and the summary banner, which was previously scoped inside the validate pane with a report's vocabulary baked into its markup. A button exists once: if a surface needs a variant the other does not have, the variant goes in the shared component. The filled button families are rust rather than the design system's accent — the system's accent was brand brick when it was written, and ‘maroon reads, rust acts’ resolved accent to maroon, so following the contract literally would have made every commit button the colour of the prose around it. Icons are Lucide, VENDORED rather than fetched: the design system's own icon component loads from a CDN and its readme flags that as the thing to change for an offline build, which for a PWA with a precache is not optional — a CDN icon set that 404s offline is a validator full of unlabelled buttons. The working set is committed and refreshed from `lucide-static` by a sync script that fails on an icon upstream renamed or one vendored but no longer named. Emoji in product UI are now a build failure rather than a review note, with the design system's sanctioned Unicode glyphs — the theme toggle's sun and moon, the verdict marks, the paging arrows — allowlisted so the rule bans the thing and not the vocabulary. ([#418](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/418))

**laterite.dev is a real page, and it shows AGS4 rather than describing it.** A masthead closed by the strata hairline, a hero, four linked AGS4 group tables you can edit and break, the file they emit, the findings the shipped validator returns for it, an install card per distribution channel, and a borehole rail that turns scrolling the page into descending a hole. PROJ → LOCA → SAMP → LLPL are drawn at their **full KEY chains** in dictionary order, sliced out of `ags_dictionary.json` at build time — which is why LLPL is a nine-column table and why `SAMP_ID` appears in three of the four. That repetition IS the relationship: AGS4 has no ids and no joins, so a child group restates its parent's key verbatim, and the page lets that land rather than hiding it. Editing is live with no submit, at every width including 390px, via a pinned key column and a row carousel; the policy that hides interactive demos below 820px is retired for this page, because a landing page whose one interactive proof is switched off for mobile visitors does not land. The engine is the slim browser build, dynamically imported on first interaction — a visitor who came to copy an install command never fetches it, and nothing is uploaded either way.

**A seeded delivery that fails in exactly four ways, and a gate that keeps it that way.** The demo's argument is “here is a real delivery, and here is what the engine thinks of it”, which dies if the engine thinks a dozen things the page never mentions. The delivery drawn in the site design tripped rules 7, 8, 10a (×5), 10c, 14, 15, 16 and 17, of which one was deliberate — and its most interesting seeded defect, a lab row pointing at a sample that does not exist, **never fired**: `LLPL` was drawn missing four of its seven KEY headings, so Rule 10c degraded to “Could not check parent entries” and the orphan story was unreachable. The committed fixture now fails on exactly a 2DP ground level given one decimal, an undefined `SAMP_TYPE` abbreviation, a missing `TRAN` group, and that orphan. Rule 16 fires **twice** for the one bad cell, because the value rides in `LLPL`'s key tuple, and the page shows both rather than deduping. The gate asserts that finding set by identity rather than by count, pins 10c to “unmatched parent key” rather than “unrunnable check”, and fails if a dictionary edition bump changes any group's KEY set.

**The install grid cannot advertise a package that is not published.** `tools/gen_install_channels.py` generates laterite.dev's five install cards from the manifests that decide each name — the wheel's pyproject, laterite-node's package.json, `prepare-wasm-package.sh` — and cross-checks every one against a second record before writing the file, so no package name is retyped into markup. A landing page naming a package the registry does not have is worse than no landing page. It refused twice before shipping: the ticket specified “the CLI on crates.io”, but `laterite-cli` is `publish = false` and has never been there (`lat` ships with the wheel and in the GitHub release), and the wheel README's Browser row named the web app where the grid names `@laterite/ags4-wasm`. `--check` runs as a CI drift gate.

**A separation gate beside the contrast gate.** `contrast.test.ts` asks whether a colour is legible ON a ground; it never asked whether two colours are legible AGAINST EACH OTHER, and every defect fixed here passed it. The new `separation.test.ts` measures ΔE in OKLab under normal, protan and deutan vision (Machado–Oliveira–Fernandes 2009 at severity 1.0, which is part of the standard rather than an implementation detail) and holds the chart palette to the dataviz method's six checks on both pairlists, every chart slot clear of every status colour, the semantic layer against itself, the elevation ladder to a ΔL floor, and — closing a gap the docs opened — the syntax-highlighting colours against `--surface-code`, the surface they actually sit on. The two pairs that cannot be fixed are pinned at their measured values as ratchets, so they may improve and not decay. Hue angle is deliberately NOT the measure: it scored the pair that started this at 29° apart and safe while they were ΔE 1.1 and indistinguishable. (#434)

changed.text: **laterite is in beta.** One claim covering everything shipped, replacing four enumerations in the repo that disagreed about which surfaces exist. PyPI's `Development Status` classifier moves from `3 - Alpha` to `4 - Beta` — the only machine-readable status field the project owns; npm, crates.io and the web app have no equivalent field, so they carry the claim as a README line and a footer link instead of in a `description`, which is read while deciding whether to click and cannot carry the explanation that makes the claim fair. The Rust crate `laterite` is the one exception, and for completeness rather than quality: it is not yet at parity with the other five surfaces (`dec-facade-parity` phase 4 of 9) and joins when it is — it runs the same engine they do.

**The Excel crate is `laterite-ags4-excel`.** It was `laterite-excel` — a name chosen for the general-purpose Excel library it was meant to become and never did. `-ags4-` marks the engine tier and bare `laterite-*` is for the format-agnostic crates, of which `laterite-transport` is the only genuine one; this crate holds contents its own header calls AGS4-specific. Renamed **now** because a crates.io name is free until its first publish and irreversible after, and this crate is scheduled to publish — the same reasoning that renamed `laterite-ags4-check` to `laterite-cli` before the engine tier went out. Nothing a user types changes: the Python, Node, browser and `lat excel` surfaces are untouched, and the crate has never been on a registry for anyone to depend on. Internally the lib name moves with it, so `laterite_excel::` becomes `laterite_ags4_excel::` at every call site. Past release entries here carry the new name too, deliberately: one grep gives one answer rather than an exception list to carry forward.

**`tests/test_docs_node_api.py` now also scans the npm landing page.** Falsification of the new executor found the gap: a bare `report.someTypo` evaluates to `undefined` and logs rather than throwing, so executing cannot catch it, and the static gate scanned `docs/node/` only — leaving `laterite-node/README.md` covered by neither. The executor catches calls, the resolver catches reads; neither subsumes the other.

**The compiled dependency set moves forward: arrow 59.1 → 59.2, PyO3 0.29.0 → 0.29.2, napi 3.12.0 → 3.12.1 (with `napi-derive` 3.6.1 → 3.6.3 and `napi-build` 2.4.0 → 2.4.1), `thiserror` 2.0.19 → 2.0.20 and `rust_xlsxwriter` 0.97.0 → 0.97.1.** Declared here rather than waved through because this repo ships BUILT artefacts — these are the versions actually inside the wheel, the Node addon, the wasm bundle and `lat`, not ranges a consumer's own resolver gets to pick from. All are patch or minor moves within the existing manifest ranges, so only `Cargo.lock` changes; no API a caller touches moves with them. The arrow bump was additionally checked against the co-residency fault fixed earlier in this cycle — `import pyarrow` then `import laterite`, with pyarrow 25.0.0, still hands back intact buffers under the mimalloc v2 pin.

**Breaking: the Node package requires Node >= 22.** `engines` said `>=18` for fifteen months and was never true — an unverified guess rather than a support commitment, with nothing in CI testing Node 18 or 20. It now equals the tested floor, with Node 24 added to the matrix beside it. Done now rather than later because there is no user to break, and the cost of correcting the number will never be lower.

**The compatibility promise now says which surface it is about.** "laterite is in beta, and pre-1.0 a minor may break you" and "this crate exists so that reshaping does not reach you" were both true, both shipped, and being printed apart — four lines from each other, about the same crate. They are one statement in two clauses now: the facade absorbs *engine* reshaping, and its own surface is pre-1.0 and may break you. The docs site's `reference/support.md` gains **How versions move**, which states the rule once for the three version lines actually running — the product line (one number, one changelog, minor-for-breaking, in beta), the Rust crate (its own clock, outside the beta claim, changes faster), and the engine crates (no promise at all: machinery, not a door). "Read the changelog before upgrading" is deliberately a product-line clause only, and names root `CHANGELOG.md`, where the breaking-changes index makes it a short list rather than a read; the Rust crate gets the honest form instead — the API will change, Cargo will not carry you across a `0.x` minor on a caret requirement, don't force one — because a Rust consumer is protected by the resolver whether they read anything or not, and `pip install laterite` unpinned is not. `reference/changelog.md` now leads with `CHANGELOG.md` instead of the GitHub Releases feed, which is the artifact with a drift gate behind it.

**The site has its own home: `laterite.dev`.** The browser validator answers at `app.laterite.dev` and the documentation at `docs.laterite.dev` — two hosts, where before they rode one artifact with the docs in a subdirectory of the app. Every published link moves with them. The old `niko86.github.io/laterite/` URLs keep working: that site stays up serving nothing but redirects, which is what makes the move safe after 0.8.x and 0.9.0 froze the old host into READMEs on PyPI, npm and crates.io that can never be edited. **If you allowlist hosts, add `cdn.laterite.dev`** — the DuckDB engine behind the Explore tab is a 34-39 MiB wasm and the static-asset host caps a single file at 25 MiB, so that one file is served from object storage on the same domain. Validate, Fix and the rest are unaffected, and nothing about the privacy claim changes: no file you open has ever left the browser and none does now. Two links were already dead and are fixed on the way past: the bug template pointed reporters at the known-divergences page and the issue chooser at the feedback page, both omitting the `/docs/` segment, so the first two links anybody filing a bug follows were 404s. Nothing checks a URL that lives in an issue template. ([#332](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/332))

**Breaking: `@laterite/ags4-wasm` is the slim engine — 749 KiB gzipped instead of 1.81 MiB.** One artifact used to carry everything, so a page that only wanted to validate a file still downloaded the Excel reader/writer, Arrow IPC, the certificate stack, diff, merge and censor. Six cargo features now gate those — `excel`, `arrow`, `certify`, `diff`, `merge`, `censor` — and the published package is built with none of them: 1.8 MiB raw / 749 KiB gzip / 573 KiB brotli, against 5.1 MiB / 1.71 MiB / 1.24 MiB for the full engine. **What leaves npm is `arrow_ipc` and `build_ags4_ipc`, `ags4_to_xlsx` and `xlsx_to_ags4`, `certify`, `diff`, `merge` and `censor`**; every one is still there in a source build, because `default = full` and the features are ON by default — the app at app.laterite.dev compiles the crate itself and is unaffected. The one place this bites a caller rather than merely removing a verb is `read`: the handle's rows came back as Arrow IPC and now come back as JSON from the new `rows_json()`, through the SAME `parse_value` cast — a `2DP` heading is still a number, a `DT` still a datetime string — so the values are identical and only the framing differs. It is not a drop-in for `arrow_ipc()`, which is why this declares itself breaking. Nothing was removed from the middle of the chain: read → validate → **fix** → write is intact, and `meta()` + `rows_json()` together are exactly `build_ags4`'s input shape, so a browser round-trip composes without an adapter. Gates rather than compiler flags because the measurement said so: our own Rust is ~7.6% of the binary and `arrow` alone ~35% of its code section, while every compiler knob tried came to ~180 KB between them — `opt-level = "z"` and `"s"` were both measured and both rejected, at 13–95% slower in the browser. A gate holds the split: `tools/release/check-wasm-slim.mjs` checks the exported surface exactly, and then holds TWO ceilings, gzip and raw, because the axes answer different questions. Gzip is what a client pays. Raw is where redundant data is unmistakable — the duplicate dictionary this same release removes was +1375 KiB raw but only +98 KiB gzipped, which would have cleared a gzip-only ceiling by five kilobytes, and catching a 1.4 MB blob on five kilobytes of margin is luck rather than a gate. Neither ceiling pretends to catch a flipped feature gate: at +14 to +36 KiB gzipped for `certify`, `diff`, `censor` and `merge`, no ceiling with honest headroom would, and the surface check catches all four by name.

**The dictionary was embedded twice; now it is embedded once — 1.4 MB off every artifact.** `laterite-ags4-reference` compiles `ags_dictionary.json` into `phf` tables at build time, which is why the crate's own docs said it reads "nothing at runtime". Its `union` module did not: it carried a SECOND copy of the same 1.4 MB file via `include_str!` and parsed it on the first `registry()` call to rebuild the all-editions union. Every artifact that touched the registry paid for both — the browser wasm, the wheel's `.so`, `lat`, the Node addon. `union_groups()` now reconstructs that union from the masked tables instead (each group and heading at its newest edition, in `gen_dictionary.py`'s heading order), so nothing is stored twice: **wasm 6,722,493 → 5,312,456 raw (−21.0%)**, `lat` −18.7%, the Node addon −15.5%, the wheel's `.so` −7.1%. Behaviour is unchanged and that is asserted rather than asserted-about: the JSON stays as a `#[cfg(test)]` ORACLE, and a differential test compares the reconstruction against it across all 174 groups and ~3,500 headings — field by field, order included — because "spot-check PROJ and LOCA" would not notice a heading whose edition set moved its latest definition. It is a SIZE win and not a startup one: `union_groups()` went 2.13 ms → 1.56 ms, since both paths allocate the same owned headings and the parse was never the dominant cost. Worth saying how it hid for so long — JSON that repetitive compresses ~18:1, so the duplicate was 1.4 MB raw but only ~54 KB of what a browser actually downloads, and every compressed-size check reported it as fine. Raw size is what found it, which is the general lesson: the two axes disagree, and only one of them shows a redundant blob. A second test now fails the build if an `include_str!` of the dictionary reappears outside the oracle.

**The validator app paints without waiting for its engine.** First render was gated on the whole engine instantiating, so nothing appeared on screen until several MB of wasm had downloaded and compiled — someone who opened the app, read the page and left had paid for the Excel converter, the Arrow stack, the certificate machinery, diff, merge and censor before seeing anything. The ~30 KB tokenizer stays in the gate, because the validate and fix views tokenize lines synchronously and genuinely cannot paint without it. The engine comes out of it: its real deadline is when a *file* is loaded, not when the page paints, and a human choosing a file puts seconds between the two. **Nothing new appears on screen for this.** A file loaded before the engine has arrived waits inside Validate's existing loading state and then reports normally — "engine still arriving" and "validate in progress" are the same thing to a user, and the request queues in the worker rather than racing it. The sample-file buttons are the one path that can reach that window in milliseconds, so that is what the e2e drives: it holds the engine wasm on the wire behind a hand-released route, asserts the buttons paint while it is held, and asserts the file loaded in that window still validates once it lands. An engine that *fails* is still reported at page level, unchanged and as loudly as before: a rejection is not a wait, and leaving it to the panes turned out to be a permanent silent state rather than a quieter one. Offline behaviour is unchanged — the precache still carries the engine, so a second visit never sees the window at all. ([#360](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/360))

**Explore and Tools → Excel run in a second worker, created only when one of those tabs is opened.** Everything the app did in wasm ran in one worker, so an Explore parse and a running validate shared a queue and a process — and the handle Explore's typed data lives in sat alongside every validate. Those two features now have their own worker, and it is created when the tab is opened rather than when the page loads, so a visit that opens neither costs nothing beyond ~20 KiB of glue in the offline install. What a user can notice is small and all in one direction: opening Explore can no longer hold up a validate that is still running, and the engine behind Excel starts coming up when the tool is selected rather than when the button is pressed.
