Explore's parsed dataset moved with Explore — it is the only thing the worker holds between requests, and its only consumer is that tab — and it is still freed between parses. **Both workers deliberately still run the same engine build.** This change is the shape alone: the split that lets the second one carry the heavy engine while the first drops to a smaller, precached one is the next change, and holding them apart means a size regression there has one suspect rather than three. ([#362](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/362))

**The validator app's offline install is 38% smaller: 11.4 MiB → 7.1 MiB.** The browser precached the whole engine — 6.6 MB of wasm, including the Excel converter, the Arrow stack, the certificate machinery, diff, merge and censor — on every first visit, whether or not the visitor ever validated anything. It now precaches **tier 1** instead: the same engine minus `arrow` and `excel`, 2.1 MB raw / 839 KiB gzipped, which is everything Validate, Fix, Export and every tool but Excel actually need. The full engine still exists and is still exact; it is simply fetched the first time someone opens Explore or Tools → Excel, into the second worker those two already had, and cached there for offline use afterwards. **What works offline got bigger, not smaller** — the notice used to promise Validate and Fix, and now honestly says Validate, Fix, Export and Tools, because all of Tools is served by the precached artifact. The two engines are separate artifacts by build (`--out-name ags4_wasm_full`), and that is the load-bearing detail: both `wasm-pack` runs emit the same default filename, so without it the two would fingerprint to the same stem, the precache glob would match both, and every visitor would silently be back on the full engine with every feature working and every size ceiling green. Three locks now sit in front of that — distinct names, an explicit `globIgnores` entry, and a file-size cap dropped from 8 MiB to 3, which the smaller precached artifact finally made possible to place BETWEEN the two engines — and one end-to-end assertion that tier 2 is absent from the precache, which is the only one of the four that fails a test rather than printing a warning. It was falsified before being trusted. ([#364](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/364))

**Explore and Tools → Excel no longer start a 5.2 MB download on the click.** Tier 2 — the full engine, which only those two tabs need — was fetched the first time one of them was opened, so the first open paid for the download in front of the user. It is now warm-fetched during idle time instead, so on most visits the bytes are already cached by the time anyone gets there. It rides the **existing** idle-warm policy rather than a second one of its own: the same Data Saver bail and the same low-end-device check that already gate the DuckDB warm, so a metered or constrained device downloads nothing speculatively and simply waits on the click, as before. Two properties are easy to get wrong and are held by tests rather than by intent. The warm **fetches and stops** — it never instantiates, because compiling ~5 MB of wasm for two tabs most visitors never open would hand back a good part of what the tiering won, so the compile still waits for the worker that opening one of those tabs creates. And it starts only **after tier 1 is up**, never alongside it: tier 1 is on the critical path and this is speculative, and fetching them together lets the speculative one steal bandwidth from the needed one — a delay that would land exactly on the sample-file path, where someone can go from cold paint to needing the engine in milliseconds. A failed warm is silent and costs nothing: the tab that needs the engine still fetches it. ([#365](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/365))

**laterite.dev is a real build now, on the shared design tokens.** The apex was one hand-written HTML file served as assets by a Worker with no code — the right shape for a placeholder that only had to stop the redirect shim pointing at a hostname with no record, and the wrong one for the page it is becoming. It has its own Vite build under `web/landing/` now, sharing the web project's single dependency set and nothing else, and its deploy step consumes that build rather than the file. The copy and the three destinations are unchanged; what changed under them is the type and the colour. Deliberately NOT a second entry in the app's build: that config carries a PWA registration layer, an SPA 404 fallback and a step that relocates the oversized DuckDB wasm out to R2, none of which belong on a small static page — and two entries sharing a chunk graph would let the app's heavy dependencies reach the apex unnoticed, which is the exact failure the separation exists to prevent. A check fails the landing build if one does, and it is written as an allowlist inverted rather than a denylist, so adding DuckDB, Arrow, ECharts or Leaflet to the app fences the apex off from it on the same commit. The tokens live in a shared directory both builds resolve, extending the app's existing semantic vocabulary rather than introducing a parallel one — every name the app had, this has. Figtree, Public Sans and IBM Plex Mono are self-hosted and subset: the page whose pitch is that nothing is uploaded now fetches nothing from a third-party font origin either. Light values are populated; the dark set is a values change into a slot that already exists. ([#417](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/417))

**One theme mechanism, not two.** `ThemeToggle` and the theme store moved from the browser app into the shared layer when laterite.dev's masthead needed a theme control. Both surfaces now resolve the theme the same way — a stored choice falling back to the OS preference, applied pre-paint from an inline script so there is no flash, mirrored to a class on the root element so an explicit choice can beat the OS **in both directions**, which a `prefers-color-scheme` media query alone cannot express. Same storage key on both, so a reader who set the theme in the web app arrives at the landing page with it already applied. The landing page also gains its dark values: the band ramp shifts one step lighter (the deep strata vanish on a dark canvas), tints dial down from 26/18% to 20/14%, cards lift by surface step rather than shadow, the mark takes a plate on dark chrome — and the rust CTA is identical in both themes, which is what makes it read as the action everywhere.

**The app wears the site's design: `app.laterite.dev` moves onto the shared tokens and the pairing's type.** The validator now draws its colours from the same token layer as `laterite.dev`, in both themes — the app's neutrals were already routed through one semantic layer, so the restyle is the values changing underneath the components rather than the components changing. Type moves with it: Public Sans for the interface, IBM Plex Mono for AGS data and code, Figtree on the masthead — self-hosted and subset like the rest of the site, so the app still loads from exactly one origin and works offline. The theme toggle, its persistence and its no-flash first paint are untouched. Two dark-theme defects were fixed on the way: the commit-action colour silently shifted hue in dark by riding the band ramp's dark shift, and its tinted wash was the one wash the dark pass never dimmed, glowing on the near-black canvas. Contrast across the foreground ramp, the status text and the action pair is now held by a test in both themes rather than sampled by eye. ([#422](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/422))

**docs.laterite.dev runs the same pairing as the apex and the app.** The docs were the last surface on stock Material — deep orange on Roboto, pulled from a third-party font origin on a site whose product claims it does not phone anywhere. They now render on the shared token layer: warm canvas, maroon headlines that follow the accent into sand on dark, IBM Plex Mono for code and AGS codes, and a dark masthead closed by the strata hairline the apex uses. Material routes its whole theme through about sixty `--md-*` variables, so this is a mapping rather than a restyle — one file points those names at ours and every page follows, including the generated catalogue pages nobody opens in review. Two of Material's own conventions had to be worked around and are written down where they bite: its defaults are declared on `<body>` as well as `:root`, so for inherited properties they beat a `:root` override by proximity rather than specificity; and each admonition type is painted at three selectors, so the obvious override leaves stock blue titles under correctly coloured borders. The left nav is band-keyed — each top-level section takes the next colour from the strata ramp, and the active item carries its section's band as a 3px inset rule — which is safe only because of one constraint that is now a gate rather than a convention: band colour appears in the nav, the table-of-contents rail, the masthead hairline and the catalogue's cap, and nowhere else. On a documentation site for a validator the warm ramp and the severity palette come from the same family, so a rust-tinted callout is indistinguishable from an error; the gate caught one real case while it was being written, the syntax-highlighting colours, which now run on the status palette. The group catalogue is the site's single sanctioned spotlight, its filter and pager unchanged and its caption now reading the group count and the dictionary edition span from the registry that generates the table. The three families are self-hosted: MkDocs has no bundler, so it can follow neither the shared layer's `@import` chain nor the Fontsource specifiers inside it, and the tokens and faces are generated into the docs tree and checked in CI — a retuned colour cannot ship to two surfaces and quietly skip the third. With Material's font block switched off and its GitHub repository-facts fetch removed — two requests per browser tab, for the latest tag, stars and forks — the site loads no third-party origin at all.

**The validator app's severity tiers read without colour, and informational findings stop wearing the link colour.** The findings list states each tier in form as well as hue — a solid fill for errors, a 3px stratum tick for warnings, a hairline stencil for FYI — so a greyscale print or a colour-blind reader keeps the ranking, and the character-level hit mark inside each snippet is keyed to the same tier. FYI findings, which rendered in the interactive accent colour and read as clickable, move onto the info token — the steel of the severity filter, fix badges and rule explainer — and a report whose only findings are FYI now gets an informational verdict banner rather than a warning one. Every status, accent and tinted fill in the app resolves through the shared design tokens, and a lint gate keeps raw palette colours from coming back. (#404)

**Destructive actions in the validator app ask before they act, and its controls land on the design system's contracts.** A button that would replace or discard the loaded file — reverting applied fixes, applying the Formatter's result in place, loading a sample over an open file — now repaints to the error colour on first click and asks its question in place (“Discard all fixes?”); the second click acts, and pressing Escape, moving away, or losing focus stands it down. Keyboard focus is visible on every input, including in forced-colours mode, where the old treatment vanished entirely; disabled controls dim instead of repainting grey; hover and press change colour only; and corner radii resolve through the shared token scale per object class — inputs tightest, chips the one soft step. The update prompt, the app's one floating surface with a generic shadow, becomes the system's dark toast. Every transition routes through the shared motion tokens, so a reduced-motion preference now stops all animation in the app, the loading spinner included, and a lint gate keeps untokened shadows, blurs, motion values and suppressed focus styles from returning. (#408)

**The landing page joins the design system's gates, and its chrome stops frosting.** The masthead was a 95%-alpha surface over a backdrop filter — the last blurred surface anywhere, against a system whose stated rule is that nothing is blurred. It is opaque now, which also spares a compositor layer for a job the strata rule beneath it already does: saying the chrome is in front. The depth pill on the borehole rail and the plate behind the brand mark were reaching for Tailwind's stock stone, a COOL grey, while every other neutral in the product comes from the warm ramp — close enough to pass a glance, far enough to read as a grey chip beside a warm mark. The pill now takes one theme-flipping token in place of a light/dark foreground pair, and the plate references the warm ramp directly. Three focus rings in the interactive demo suppressed their outline outright rather than hiding it, which loses the ring entirely in forced-colors mode, where the box-shadow that replaced it is discarded. With those gone, both design gates — the palette one and the elevation/motion/state one — now cover the landing as well as the app, and the exemption that carved it out is deleted rather than merely unused.

**The validator app's chrome lands on the design system: the lockup, one centred column, and data regions that stop growing the page.** The header now reads the way every laterite surface signs itself — the mark, the brand word in the display face, a hairline divider, then “AGS4 Validator” in the UI face with the explorer as a muted qualifier — in place of a product name set in display weight, which is the arrangement the system warns reads as packaging; on dark chrome the mark sits on its light plate so the outline separates. Header, tab strip, content and footer centre on one shell column with fixed gutters, the tab bar's hairline running full-width beneath the centred strip with the active tab's accent underline sitting on it. And the long data regions that still grew the page — the Fix tab's whole-file diff and per-fix list, the revision-diff and merge outputs, the Explore overview, the export and template previews — now cap their height and scroll internally, stepping up on larger viewports, with table headers held visible while scrolling: a ten-thousand-row delivery no longer produces a ten-thousand-row page. (#407)

**The Validate and Fix panes compose from the design system's primitives, and applying fixes asks first.** The dictionary, encoding and aligned-columns controls become real form fields with the system's field wrapper and control metrics; every toolbar action in both panes — the certificate and report downloads, the file chooser, the encoding switches, undo, the download — is the shared button in its proper variant rather than bespoke markup. In the findings list each rule's header now wears an instrument chip carrying the rule number, toned by the worst severity in that rule's findings, so a rule that raises one error among warnings reads as an error rule at a glance; each proposed fix states the line it anchors to beside its rule link. And because applying fixes rewrites the loaded file, the apply actions now take the armed-confirm contract the rest of the app adopted: the first press repaints the button and turns its label into the question, the second acts, and stepping away stands it down. (#409)

**The Explore and Tools panes finish the app's move onto the design system — every remaining control a primitive, charts on tokens, the map's chrome included.** The explore surface (data table, results grid, SQL console and builder, chart builder, export bar) and the whole tools tree (dictionary browser, rule explainer, template generator, coordinate tool and map, Excel converter, formatter, merge, revision diff, anonymiser, transport) compose from the shared Button/Input/Select/Checkbox primitives in their proper variants; the deliberate exceptions — the prominent search role, hidden file-selector labels, link-idiom text buttons, rich in-label checkboxes — each carry their reason in place. Chart colours now resolve from the tokens at draw time rather than a library default palette, with one categorical sequence serving both themes (the token vocabulary cannot seat a fully CVD-clean dark trio — recorded as #434). Leaflet's own chrome — zoom control, attribution strip, popups — is brought onto the tokens by an override sheet that rides the map's lazy chunk, so the one third-party panel no longer wears library defaults. The dictionary browser's caption states both of its counts (groups and headings) derived from the loaded edition, so a dictionary edit changes them with no code edit. The only tool that replaces the loaded file (the formatter's Apply) was already behind the armed confirm; the rest download. (#410)

**Charts get their own fenced colour vocabulary, and the status tokens that collided with each other are separated.** The chart palette was cut from the brand ramp, which is a SEQUENTIAL scale — one hue family, monotone lightness — so a categorical channel built on it collapsed on the dark surface no matter how the steps were ordered. `--chart-1..5` now live in their own `shared/styles/charts.css`, fenced one-directionally: nothing there is aliased into the semantic layer and nothing there reads from it, with slot 1 pinned to the CTA by assertion rather than by `var()` so a CTA retune fails a test instead of silently repainting series 1. The hues are Paul Tol's `muted` scheme, minus the sand and olive that crowd `--warn`, snapped to each theme's lightness band. Slots 1–3 are validated on the all-pairs pairlist for scatter, where any two marks can be neighbours; all five are validated adjacent-only for bar and line. Pointing the same measure at the semantic layer found what no gate was asking about: dark `--warn` and `--accent` were ΔE 1.1 apart under deuteranopia — a link and a warning the same colour — and `--info` and `--ok` 1.2 apart under protanopia, because both were low-chroma and a cone deficiency removes the only channel between them. `--warn` steps up in LIGHTNESS to a pale gold rather than sideways out of amber, since status hues are semantically pinned and lightness is the channel a cone deficiency leaves intact; `--info` becomes steel blue rather than steel grey, which is where every design system that publishes its reasoning puts the informative slot. `--chip` in dark sat ΔL 0.002 from `--surface-raised` and moves above it. Light `warn`/`err` is left alone and recorded as accepted: both must clear AA as text on near-white, which forces them into the same dark warm region, and both always ship with an icon and a label. (#434)

**The repo-hygiene gates no longer wait on a Rust build.** Most of the root `tests/` suite reads files and compares them, and the six generated-view drift gates (`gen_changelog`, `gen_observations`, `gen_modality`, `gen_crate_graph`, `gen_install_channels`, `check_doc_refs`) are `--no-project` and stdlib-only — yet all of it ran in the `python` job, behind a cdylib download and `cargo build --release`, so a stale `CHANGELOG.md` took two minutes to report a string comparison. They now ALSO run in a new `repo-gates` job that installs nothing and finishes in about three seconds, alongside `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`, which never needed a wheel either. `repo-gates` is a fast head start, not a division of labour: the `python` job still runs the whole suite, because narrowing it to the complement looked tidy and quietly opened a hole — `test_landing_demo_delivery` `importorskip`s the wheel per test, so its eleven wheel-dependent tests would have been deselected in one job and skipped in the other, running nowhere while both reported green. Which modules the fast job can take is a MARKER (`needs_env`) rather than a list in the workflow, because a list in a workflow is a second place to remember, and it is read TWICE: `-m` deselects, but deselection happens after import, and a module that raises on import takes the whole session down instead of itself. That is not hypothetical — `test_vendored_authority_faithful` imports the pinned dev-only `python_ags4`, which resolves on a developer's machine and does not on a clean runner. So `tests/conftest.py` reads the same marker off the source text before collection, and `tests/test_build_marker_faithful.py` holds all three in agreement: the two readers of the marker, and the marker against the tree on both of its axes. The job carries NO path filter on purpose: #207's lesson is that a gate must fire by declaration, and an unconditional job satisfies that more strongly than any path list, because there is no condition to get wrong. That is what lets the `code` filter finally shed the SSOT documents — `changelog.json`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `observations.json`, `OBSERVATIONS.md`, `divergences.md`, the docs stylesheets, `RELEASING.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` no longer buy a wheel build. `README.md` still does, because `test_docs_snippets` doctests it and needs the package; splitting that is the remaining half. Two guards in `tests/test_paths_filter.py` keep the bargain: one fails if `repo-gates` grows an `if:` or a `needs:`, the other if a shed path creeps back into `code`.

**A fix whose rule the validator never raised is now badged `unlabelled`, not `warning`.** The Fix tab labels each proposed fix with the severity of the finding it resolves, joining on rule and line against a parallel FYI-inclusive, uncapped report. One arm of that join still answered `warning`: the report never raised the fix's rule at all. It was kept on the theory that it covered a benign gap — a fixer repairing something the validator files under a different rule name — and it covers nothing. Every fixer is gated on its numbered rule being a key of the findings it was handed and stamps that same key onto the fix it emits, and those findings come from the same door, bytes, dictionary and encoding as the report beside them, which additionally carries the warning tier the fix pass leaves off. The state is unreachable, and the point of answering `undefined` for it is not that the badge then diagnoses anything — `unlabelled` is also what every fix wears for the beat before the labelling report lands, so it cannot single the impossible case out — but that an invented tier is indistinguishable from a real one, where a missing label is merely quiet. Nothing changes for a fix whose rule the report did raise, which — across the private corpus, the repo's own fixtures and synthetic files covering every fixable rule and every fix kind — is every fix either can produce.

removed.text: **`compat.AGS4_to_dataframe_AGS3`, which mirrored nothing.** `git log -S` over python-ags4's entire history shows no such function has ever existed, in any version — so the stub was a laterite invention, and COMPAT.md's API table listed it as mirroring an upstream function in order to claim a divergence against it. AGS3 is out of scope for this project. The real O-30 refusal is unaffected: it happens on the ordinary entry points, exactly as upstream aborts on its own AGS3 detection, and is now tested there with real AGS3-shaped input instead of through a function nobody could have called.

fixed.text: **The untyped engine-failure line doubled its prefix: "The validator failed: Error: boom".** Op-level worker failures reject as `Error` instances wrapping the worker's message, and the shared fallback stringified them whole, so the pane's noun + "failed:" met a second "Error:" from the stringification. The fallback now unwraps a plain `Error` to its message alone. A named type keeps its name — "TypeError: Failed to fetch" carries half its information there — and an error with an empty message keeps the stringified form, so the line never ends at a bare colon. (#415)

**A dead engine on the Fix tab posed as a clean file, and each pane described the failure its own way.** FixPane guarded its resources against a rejected operation but read the errors nowhere, so a crashed or undownloadable engine degraded to "Fix all safe (0)" — indistinguishable from a delivery with nothing to fix. The Fix tab now renders a failure line, and the copy is one voice: a shared helper maps the engine-unavailable load/crash split — "couldn't be downloaded — check your connection" vs "stopped" — plus a raw fallback for anything untyped, to the same sentences on Validate, Fix and Explore, each pane contributing only its own noun. Validate's failure line is that typed copy now rather than a stringified error, and Explore keeps its offline-DuckDB explanation, which is true only where the engine is not precached. (#391)

**A blocked engine fetch could break Explore permanently, on that device, with no way back but a console.** Both `CacheFirst` service-worker rules accepted `statuses: [0, 200]`, and status `0` is an OPAQUE response — what a cross-origin fetch degrades to when it is refused. `CacheFirst` never revalidates, so a single refused fetch wrote the FAILURE into the cache and kept it. It is worse than serving something stale: the app fetches in `cors` mode, and a cached opaque response cannot be given to a cors request, so every later fetch threw `TypeError: Failed to fetch` — fixing the server changed nothing, and the only recovery was `caches.delete('ags-duckdb-wasm')` typed into a console by someone who knew the cache's name. That is exactly what made 2026-08-16 expensive: the CDN bucket shipped without CORS, the block lasted minutes, the poisoned cache lasted until each user cleared it by hand. Both rules now take `[200]` only. Dropping `0` is safe because nothing on these paths is opaque — the CDN answers with `access-control-allow-origin`, the OSTN15 grid is same-origin, and the app makes no `no-cors` fetch anywhere — and getting that wrong would have been silent in the other direction, with the entry never written and `CacheFirst` re-pulling 36 MB on every single page load. So it was verified as behaviour rather than as configuration: A/B on the BUILT `sw.js` in a real browser, where `[0, 200]` writes the opaque entry and the app's normal fetch then throws, and `[200]` refuses it while a healthy 200 still caches. Guarded in two places, because one instrument cannot see both directions: `web/src/lib/sw-cache-policy.test.ts` asserts the POLICY over every runtime rule — including one that omits `cacheableResponse` entirely, the same bug spelled differently — because the next such rule gets written by copying one of these; and a Playwright case asserts the BEHAVIOUR, that the engine still reaches its cache, which is the silent direction and the one no config assertion can see.

**The wheel could corrupt pyarrow's memory just by being imported.** `import pyarrow` followed by `import laterite` was enough to leave a subsequently-built `pyarrow.Table` holding zeroed bytes — no laterite call on the path, and no Arrow FFI involved. The damage was silent until some later native call tripped over it, so for months it surfaced as an intermittent SIGSEGV blamed on whichever innocent test ran next, never on the thing that caused it. pyarrow bundles its own mimalloc as its default memory pool and the `mimalloc` crate defaults to v3, and two co-resident v3 instances hand out overlapping memory (microsoft/mimalloc#1327; apache/arrow GH-50428 is the same fault from Arrow's side — a pyarrow 24.0.0 regression fixed in 25.0.1, whose own recommended workaround is the pin taken here). All three native surfaces — the wheel, the Node addon and `lat` — now pin mimalloc v2. Only pyarrow-bearing installs were ever affected (`[pyarrow]`, `[compat,pyarrow]`, `[all]`); polars and duckdb are unaffected, so the base install was never exposed. Keeping the allocator was the point: v2 holds ~18-19% read and ~14-15% validate over the system allocator, which dropping mimalloc would have given back.

**`COMPAT.md` documented a `check_file` keyword that has never existed, and a version frozen nine releases back.** Both blocks of the error-handling section passed `dictionary='not-a-dict.txt'`; the parameter is `standard_AGS4_dictionary` in laterite *and* in python-ags4, so the two snippets illustrating the divergence raised `TypeError` on both sides and showed the reader nothing — the prose was correct, only the code was uncopyable. The `laterite.compat.__version__` doctest, the `Metadata.Checker` banner a user sees in their own validation report, and the phase-1 illustration all still said `0.1.0`. `bump-my-version` stamps those two strings in `compat.py` and had no `COMPAT.md` entry, so code and page provably diverged on every release; neither superseded-version gate could catch it, because both match versions listed in `changelog.json` and its history starts at 0.6.0. The page is now stamped, and `tests/test_docs_snippets.py` asserts it against the wheel's real values.

**`gen_doc_outputs.py` silently under-counted a page that included an example SECTION.** The include→example map registered the literal `:cmd` spelling beside the bare filename, so the first page to use any other section name fell through the `not in wanted` branch as "a surface this run didn't ask for" — pointing three pages at `…py:code` dropped the matched-block count from 38 to 35 and still reported success. The key is now the include with its section suffix stripped, which covers every section name there will ever be.

**The PEP 723 pin gate could not see the file that motivated it.** It matched `laterite==(version)` and compared the version, which passes anything that is not an exact pin at all — so `examples/laterite_tour.py` asking for `laterite>=0.5.0` at product 0.10.1 (five minors of compatibility it claimed and nobody had tested) produced no match and therefore no finding, and a bare `"laterite"` escaped identically. The gate now asserts the whole specifier, discovers across both example trees rather than the docs corpus alone, and admits the `[extras]` group that the pandas examples need — `bump-version.sh` was equally blind to `laterite[compat]==`, which would have frozen those two pins at the old version while every sibling moved.

**`learn/install.md` printed its findings table in the wrong renderer.** The first page a new user reads showed plain ASCII pipes (`Rule | Line | Group`) — what the wheel's Python `lat` console script renders — on a page documenting the Rust binary, which draws comfy-table box-drawing. The row's content was correct, so somebody ran it once and nothing re-ran it: exactly the drift the CLI example gate was built for, in the blocks that gate never covered because no example backed them.

**Three crates.io READMEs documented Rust that does not compile.** `laterite-ags4-parse` iterated `parsed.groups` — a `BTreeMap` — as though it were a sequence, so `group.code` was a field access on a `(&String, &ParsedGroup)` tuple; `laterite-ags4-core` called `read_ags4_bytes(&bytes, opts)`, which takes one argument (the two-argument form is `read_ags4_bytes_with`); and `laterite-transport` called `lock(src, dest, pw, level)`, which takes five — the scrypt `log_n` was missing. A published version's README is frozen on crates.io, and `check_doc_refs.py` already treated those pages as a strict special case for their links; their code was checked by nothing.

**`node/index.md` documented `buildAgs4` with an input it rejects.** The page showed `buildAgs4({ PROJ: [{ PROJ_ID: "P1" }] })`; the signature is `AgsGroup | Map<string, GroupData> | Array<[string, GroupData]>`, so a reader copying it got `TypeError: items is not iterable`. Confirmed against the built package before fixing, and the page now shows a `Map` with a note that a plain object is not one of the accepted shapes.

**`sql()` and `at()` were unreachable for anyone installing the npm package.** `peerDependencies: { "@duckdb/node-api": ">=1.5.0" }` matched ZERO of that package's 56 published versions: every release carries a prerelease suffix (`1.5.5-r.3`, …), and semver excludes a prerelease from a range unless a comparator shares its major.minor.patch AND carries a prerelease itself — so `>=1.5.0` matched nothing, and neither did `>=1.5.0-0` or even `*`. All three install orders were reproduced against the published package: `npm i laterite` then `npm i @duckdb/node-api` (the exact command the library's own error text prints) fails with ETARGET; installing both in one command drops the peer silently; installing the peer first has it actively removed when laterite arrives. The range is now `>=1.5.5-0`, the devDependency is aligned to the same line, and the documented flow was verified end to end — install resolution against a packed build, and `sql()`/`at()` actually running against the published one. No existing gate could see this: `npm ci` installs from the lockfile, so the peer range is never consulted.

**The docs quoted a `compat` speedup lower than the one the benchmark measures.** Three docs-site pages and the wheel's own `pyproject.toml` comment said `laterite.compat` runs “~2× faster than python-ags4”. The published table in the wheel README measures 2.9×, 3.5×, 3.2×, 3.3× and 3.3× across its five file sizes — every rung above 2.9, so the prose understated the product on all of them, on the first page a python-ags4 user reads. The two figures were never the same measurement: the `~2×` dates from the 2026-07-20 Arrow pass and comes from a bench whose fixture is three data groups, where the README table is the same public call across five sizes of a 123-group scaffold. Reader-facing text now takes the published figure; the two wiki pages still carrying the old number name the fixture it belongs to instead of having a digit swapped under them, because a measurement nobody re-ran must not be quietly restated as a different one. Nothing ties prose to that table, which is why it drifted for a month — tracked as [#327](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/issues/327). ([#326](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/326))

**The published list of python-ags4 divergences is generated now, and it had been wrong in five places.** `reference/divergences.md` is the page an evaluating reader meets, and it was hand-written against `observations.json` — a source of truth that is generated and gated everywhere else in the repo. It told readers the external `--dict` override “is deferred” a release after laterite-dev#568 shipped it; four more rows carried supersession the page did not reflect; and it had never gained O-49 or O-50. It is rendered from the catalogue now, with the same drift gate the rest of that render already had. Two things changed for a reader beyond the corrections: the headline count is computed rather than asserted (**17** records change what you see, where the page claimed 19 and neither number was checkable), and the page groups by what actually happened instead of filing everything under “Known divergences from python-ags4” — a title that was wrong about four of its own rows, since O-1 and O-32 are cases where laterite *matches* python-ags4 and both depart from the spec, and O-31 and O-33 are laterite's own false negatives that the comparison caught and closed. ([#320](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/issues/320))

**A tier-2 engine that cannot be downloaded is reported on the tab that needed it, and its retry actually re-attempts.** The browser app precaches a slim engine and fetches the full one only when Explore or Tools → Excel is opened, so a failure there is partial — Validate, Fix, Export and the rest of Tools are untouched. Neither half of “report and offer a retry” worked, for two unrelated reasons. Explore never reported: it sat on “Parsing your file…” for ever, because reading a failed data source throws and the tab read it from places no error branch could guard, so the throw took the update down before the message could paint. And a retry could not have helped anyway — the worker whose engine failed keeps answering every later request from the same settled failure, so it failed identically however long ago the cause was fixed. That worker is now retired the moment its engine fails, so the next attempt starts a fresh one and downloads again, and a retry after the network returns succeeds without a page reload. Both tabs report and offer that retry, and the download failure is distinguished from an operation that ran and failed — so the retry is offered for the failure a retry can clear, and not for a conversion that failed on the file itself.

**An engine worker that dies no longer takes its tab down with it — the tab reports, offers a retry, and the next attempt gets a fresh worker.** The browser app runs its engine in workers, and a worker that crashes or whose script never loads used to be kept and reused: the requests in flight when it died reported, and every request after them was posted into something that would never answer. Nothing rejects, so nothing shows an error — the Explore tab in particular reached it on its very first parse, because opening the tab starts the worker before anything asks it for work, and sat on “Parsing your file…” indefinitely. A dead worker is now retired the way one whose engine failed to download already was, so each attempt reports instead of the first one reporting and the rest waiting. The two are distinguished where it matters: an engine that never downloaded is worth checking your connection over, and one that stopped is not, so the tab says which happened rather than guessing. One worker dying still leaves the other's tabs working, which is why the app runs two.

**Tools → Transport no longer wedges when its worker dies — the failure reports, and the next click gets a fresh worker.** The transport pane (zstd + age lock/unlock) had its own hand-rolled copy of the worker-lifecycle code the other panes moved off in #357, and the copy kept a dead worker's handle: the requests in flight when it died reported, but every attempt after them was posted into the corpse and never settled — the spinner span forever with the error branch unreachable, exactly the shape #363 fixed for the engine workers. The copy is gone: the pane's client now drives the same shared channel, which retires a dead worker so a plain retry spawns a fresh one. Deliberately no banner and no dedicated retry button — the pane already renders the failure it is handed, and the next click is the recovery.

**The wheel's `lat` renders merge's revision audit the way the Rust binary does — `["X"]`, never Python's `['X']`.** The launcher's contract is byte-faithful output to the shipped binary, and the audit line is where it silently wasn't: no test had ever merged two files that actually differ, so the line had never been rendered by anything and an interpolated Python list repr sat there unobserved. Found while wiring the released-wheel docs leg (#282), fixed with the audit's lists rendered element-by-element in the binary's own quoting, and pinned by a test that merges a fixture pair differing in exactly one cell — proven byte-identical against the binary on the same input.

**A warm still in flight doubled the download when its engine's tab was opened.** The idle warm exists to make the first Explore or Tools → Excel click fast: it primes the tier-2 engine (several MB) and DuckDB (~36 MB) into their CacheFirst buckets while the browser is idle. But `CacheFirst` does no request coalescing, so a click landing while the warm was still downloading started a second full download of the same bytes — the two split the connection, and the click the warm existed to speed up arrived slower than it would have with no warm at all, precisely on the slow links where the megabytes hurt most. The guard built with the warm covered only one direction — a warm firing after the worker exists is skipped — because the mirror cannot be closed from the main thread: the warm holds no handle a later worker could join. The one place every fetch of these artifacts already passes through is the service worker, so it is hand-written now (vite-plugin-pwa's `injectManifest` — the generated mode's rules cannot carry a custom handler; the precache manifest, its globs and their locks are unchanged, and the test holding the tier-2 engine out of the precache still fails on a leak) and every CacheFirst route coalesces in-flight requests: a request for a URL already downloading waits for that download's cache write to settle, then serves from cache. The release point is the write, not the response — at the response the body is still streaming, the cache is still empty, and the second download starts anyway. One download, however many askers, for both engines and every path that creates a worker. Held end to end by tests that pin the warm's download open at route level and open the tab mid-flight, falsified against the generated worker first: both engines measurably downloaded twice. What remains, named at the guard: a page the service worker does not yet control (the cold first visit) has nothing that can merge two downloads.

**A rejected validate froze the Validate tab on the previous file's report, with its own error message unreachable.** A Solid resource throws when read after a failure, and ValidatePane read its report from an effect, two eager memos and the results `<Show>` itself — so the moment an op rejected (a worker crash, or the engine throwing inside a dispatch), the throw took the whole update down before the pane's own "Validator error" fallback could render. What stayed on screen was whatever had last painted — at worst the PREVIOUS file's "Clean — 0 findings" over the NEW file's text, a stale verdict posing as a fresh one, with the only trace an uncaught page error. Every report read now routes through one guarded accessor, the shape Explore got when the identical trap took that tab down (the dec-engine-tiering warning box), and the fallback checks guard-first — loading, then error, then the empty state — so the error branch is reachable and a retry in flight reads as validating. The same accessor landed on the eager readers next door: FixPane's severity memos and reseed effect, and ChartBuilder's option memo, whose own error banner sat behind the identical throw. No retry button was added, because none is needed — the worker channel already retires a crashed engine, so the user's next input validates on a fresh one. Guarded by an e2e that kills the live tier-1 worker and blocks its replacement's chunk — shown red against the unguarded pane, frozen exactly as described — and asserts the page-level dead-engine banner stays silent, because a crash after boot belongs to the pane that felt it (#359).

**A fix engine that died mid-labelling left every fix badged `warning`.** The Fix tab runs two operations on one worker: the fixes themselves, and a parallel validation whose only job is labelling each fix with the severity of the finding it resolves. A crashed worker rejects only the requests still waiting on it, so when the labelling reply was the one in flight, the tab kept a real, applicable list of fixes and lost the report that explains them — and the severity join, asked about a report that was never there, answered `warning` for all of them. Error-backed and FYI-backed fixes became indistinguishable at exactly the moment nothing had classified them. The join now separates the two ways a severity can be missing: no report at all reads as `unlabelled` and says so on the badge, while a report that simply doesn't raise a given rule keeps its long-standing default. The same guard covers a report that is still arriving, which went wrong two ways: on the first file every badge read `warning`, and on every file after it the badges were drawn from the PREVIOUS file's report until the new one landed — a confident label sourced from different bytes. Both now read `unlabelled` until the report for those bytes arrives. Fix badges moved onto the shared chip in the same change, so the three severities differ in form and not only in colour — readable without colour, as the findings list already was.

**A family of design-token styles that silently never applied now does.** Tailwind's v4 line dropped the older shorthand that wrapped a square-bracketed token reference in `var()`, so utilities written that way compiled to invalid declarations every browser discards — the class sat in the markup looking applied while the style never rendered. In the validator app that was the dialog's dimming scrim, the toast and tooltip fills and shadows, and control heights; on the landing page, the strata band keying and the display tracking. All of them now use the supported reference form, verified against the built stylesheets, and a lint gate keeps the broken shorthand from coming back.

**A delivery carrying hundreds of fixes no longer mounts hundreds of fix cards.** The Fix tab's scroll cap (#407) bounded the *page* — the cards scroll inside it while the Apply bar stays put — but bounded nothing about what mounted: every fix still built its card, and every card a full aligned GROUP diff block, tens of thousands of DOM nodes with almost all of them off-screen at any moment. The safe list is now windowed the way the findings list one tab over already was, mounting only the visible slice plus its overscan, with the same measured-size resets the findings list learned the hard way. The risky group — small, opt-in, and read whole before ticking anything in it — keeps its plain rendering below the window, and nothing about the cap or the Apply bar moved. (#435)

**Fenced code blocks were invisible in the docs' light theme.** `--surface-code` is tuned to sit on `--surface`, but the docs read long-form on `--canvas`, and it lands ΔL 0.001 from it — contrast ratio 1.00. The block had also been given `border: none` on the reasoning that "a fenced block is already an object", which is true only where its fill reads. Retuning the token cannot fix this: it would have to clear both grounds while dodging `--surface-raised` and `--chip`, and the light ladder's five steps span L 0.891–0.978 with no gap that size. One global fill cannot serve three surfaces with three different page grounds, so form carries it — the hairline is back, and line-numbered blocks take the frame on the table rather than down the middle of the two cells. (#434)

**A chart coloured by any column with more values than the palette has slots drew two different series in the same colour, and the default form was already using pairs the separation gate had never checked for it.** The Explore chart builder split rows into one series per distinct value of the colour-by column and handed the whole palette to ECharts, with nothing bounding the split — and the colour-by control offers any column, so a real delivery's location type, geology code or sample type routinely overran it. Past the last slot ECharts neither fails nor derives a hue: its palette mixin advances modulo the palette length, so the series after the last one is repainted the FIRST slot's colour, on the same axes, under a legend saying the two differ. The lower ceiling was the live one: only the head of the slot sequence is validated on the ALL-PAIRS pairlist, where any two marks can land side by side, and the builder's default chart type is scatter — so the common case was past its real limit at four series, not six. Colour was also assigned in series order, which is first-appearance order in the fetched rows, so changing the plotted set repainted the survivors and silently invalidated the mapping a reader carried over from the previous view. Both ceilings are now enforced rather than described: one definition of the slot count and the all-pairs head, read by the separation gate and by the builder alike, and everything past a form's cap folds into a single `Other` series painted a new neutral held to the slots' separation floors and to the inverse of their chroma rule. Which values survive is decided by a SQL cardinality probe composed from the plot query's own table, joins, aliasing and row filter — not read off the plotted rows, because the scatter query is a bare row `LIMIT` with no `ORDER BY` and a legend saying "Other" over an arbitrary slice would claim more than the sample supports. Colour follows a value's rank rather than its position, so nothing about the plotted slice — the row cap, or which rows an un-ordered `LIMIT` happens to return — can repaint a survivor. Composing the probe from the plot's own population is what costs the other half of that: a join that fans base rows out changes the counts and so can reorder the ranking, which is the trade taken deliberately, because it is what makes "Other" a claim about the delivery the chart actually draws.

**Every `dark:` utility on the landing page fired from the reader's OS rather than from the theme they had chosen.** Tailwind's default dark variant is `prefers-color-scheme`, and an entry has to override it to key off a class instead. `src/app.css` declared that override from the start; `landing/landing.css` never did — while the page's theme is `.dark` on `<html>`, applied pre-paint from the persisted-else-system choice. The two agree only for as long as a reader's OS and their choice agree, and when they diverge the utilities fire with the WRONG SET'S VALUES, because the class that switches the token values is not the thing that switched the utility on. On a dark-mode machine viewing the page in light — the state of anyone on such a machine who has ever chosen light — the demo table's card took `--surface-raised` from the LIGHT set, which on this surface is the canvas: the table the page opens with had no fill of its own at all. Fixed by declaring the same class variant the app's entry declares, and gated per-entry, which is the only granularity that can catch it — each bundle is compiled and asserted to emit no `prefers-color-scheme`, so a new entry cannot inherit Tailwind's default in silence. The same audit found the other half of the divergence: this entry excluded `*.test.ts` from the class scan but never `*.test.tsx`, which the app's entry has always excluded — so a component test, the kind that necessarily writes the classes it renders, would have shipped every one of them into the bundle. There are none today; the asymmetry between two entries that should agree is the defect, and it is closed here too.

**Both token gates read one stylesheet, so the landing page's palette had never been checked — and it was shipping a panel with no fill.** `contrast.test.ts` and `separation.test.ts` parsed `colors.css` and nothing else, while `colors.css` itself names `--canvas` as the one token a surface is expected to retune and `landing.css` takes that offer. Every threshold in both files was asserted about a palette laterite.dev does not paint. What that hid: the landing's canvas resolves to `--surface-raised`'s own value, so the row carousel's tray and the fixer's note — both filled with the raised step, both sitting directly on the canvas — had no fill of their own at all and read as bare page inside a border, on the surface with the most first-time readers. Both gates now build the RENDERED themes rather than the authored ones, overlaying each surface's own blocks in cascade order so the landing's light and dark sets are evaluated beside the shared pair; the landing's `theme-color` mirrors are held to the retuned canvas the same way the app's already were. The elevation collision is resolved without moving a token, because the light band has no room to move one into — solving it, the only legal windows for the raised step are indistinguishable from white or below `--chip`, since `--line` and `--line-subtle` close the gap it would naturally take. Instead the two panels adopt the pairing `GroupTable` already ships on this page: the lifting fill in light, the raised step in dark, and a recessing fill for the tray, which holds cards it would otherwise swallow. A rung a surface has given up is now declared on its theme set and backed by an assertion that the landing never fills with it outside a `dark:` guard, so the record cannot decay into prose.

**The bundle shipped raw palette classes that no component uses — planted by the comments that ban them.** Tailwind scans source as raw TEXT and cannot tell code from comment, so a comment naming a complete utility emits it. `eslint.config.js` cites `bg-emerald-600` and `text-sky-50` as examples of what `design/no-raw-palette` forbids, and `cursor-not-allowed` as what `design/no-raw-effects` forbids: the gates were shipping all three into the app's stylesheet. The eslint rules cannot ever catch this — they visit `Literal` and `TemplateElement` nodes, and a comment is invisible to both. Fixed by excluding the files that DISCUSS classes without rendering any: the two configs, `scripts/`, every test file, and — the one nobody had looked for — the whole MkDocs `docs-site/` prose tree, which sits under the Vite root and was being read for class names, roughly halving the number of files the app's scan reads. The guard is an OUTCOME gate rather than another source rule: `bundle-palette.test.ts` compiles each entry the way the Vite plugin does and asserts the emitted stylesheet carries no vendor-palette utility, with the family list read from tailwindcss's own theme so a new vendor colour needs no edit. That covers every route in, including the one exclusions cannot reach — a comment inside a component that does render.

**A chip had no edge, because its fill and the rule beside it were the same colour.** In light `--chip` and `--line` both resolved to `--stone-200`, and `--surface-raised` and `--line-subtle` both to `--stone-150` — so a filter chip drawn `bg-chip border-line` read as a gap in the rule rather than as an object, and a table row ruled `border-line-subtle` lost that rule the moment a raised hover filled it. Dark held distinct values for both pairs and was no better off: they differed by less than a rounding error, which is the same defect without the shared value that makes it obvious. Five values move and nothing else does. The invariant is the part worth keeping — the separation gate now asserts that a token whose job is a FILL differs from one whose job is a STROKE, which is a relation nothing measured, its elevation check comparing surface to surface. The floor is what the light neutrals can hold rather than what would be ideal: `--chip` is fenced above by `--line` and below by `--fg-dim`'s contrast floor sitting on it, so the band between `--surface-raised` and the darkest legal chip is split evenly with nothing spare, and a wider step has to move one of those two first.

added.text: **The browser package has an API reference.** `@laterite/ags4-wasm` ships to npm with fully typed results, and until now the docs site did not mention it once — the crate README was its only documentation. `reference/wasm-api.md` documents it through the practices the web app actually uses, with worked examples whose printed output is generated from running them: init once and await that promise (and pass `module_or_path` explicitly, or a non-root `base` breaks the fetch fallback), read severity through one resolver because an absent `severity` means *error*, take the types from the package rather than mirroring them, hold a `ParsedDataset` across its Arrow pulls and free it before the next parse, propose fixes before applying them, and keep the synchronous engine off the main thread.

**`laterite.dev` answers.** A deliberately thin placeholder — what the project is, and the three links that matter (the browser app, the docs, the source). It exists now because the apex was being *advertised* while serving nothing: the redirect shim left on the old GitHub Pages host names `laterite.dev` in its canonical tag and its no-JavaScript fallback, so every crawler following it, and every visitor without JavaScript, was pointed at a hostname with no record. A redirect rule would have closed that too; a Worker was chosen because the real landing page will be one, so this is the same object thinner rather than scaffolding to remove later.

changed.text: **The `lat` console script the wheel installs now renders the same tables as the shipped `lat` binary.** Two programs answer to `lat` — the Rust binary and this Python console script — and until now they printed visibly different output for the same command: comfy-table's UTF-8 box grid from one, a plain `ljust` grid from the other. The machine-readable surfaces (`--json`, `--ndjson`, `--csv`, the group listing, exit codes) had always been held byte-identical by test; the grids people actually read were pinned nowhere, which is how the divergence survived. The glyphs are now matched exactly, colour included (bold-cyan header, dim alternate rows, honouring `NO_COLOR` and a real terminal the same way the binary does), and the human table has joined the byte-parity tests instead of being excluded from them. **No new dependency:** the CLI remains stdlib-only. The two still part under an interactive TTY, where comfy-table wraps to the terminal width and this does not — a case no gate or document captures.

**The browser story is one page instead of thirteen near-identical tabs.** Each cookbook page carried a *Browser* tab saying the same three sentences — same engine, in your browser, nothing uploaded — about whichever pane of the web app was relevant. Those are consolidated into the web app's own page (`surfaces/browser.md`), which now describes what each pane gives you; the cookbook's *Available in* line links there instead. The app is a showcase for the wasm package, not a product, so it gets one page describing it and the package gets the API reference every other surface already had.

**The web app lints on ESLint 10.** It was the last surface still on 9 — `laterite-node` had already moved — and the bump was blocked by `eslint-plugin-solid`, whose peer range stops at `^9.0.0` and whose last release was December 2024. That peer is now relaxed by an `overrides` entry, which is only defensible because the thing an override can hide was checked: the plugin's rules still **fire** under 10 (a deliberate `solid/reactivity` violation is still caught), not merely load. Two of 10's new rules earned the upgrade. `preserve-caught-error` found a real defect in the wasm-tokenizer test setup, which interpolated the caught error's `.message` into a new one and dropped the original — throwing away the stack that distinguishes *nobody ran the build* from *the wasm will not instantiate*, the one moment you need to tell them apart; it now attaches `cause`. `no-unassigned-vars` flagged four Solid ref bindings, where the JSX compiler does the write the rule cannot see (and the definite-assignment `!` does not satisfy it — three of the four already carried one); it is off for `.tsx` only, so a never-assigned `let` in a plain `.ts` module stays a hard failure.

**A narrowed `AGS4_to_dataframe` no longer builds the groups it is about to throw away.** `only_groups` narrowed the *result*, but the narrowing happened in Python — the native parse had already built and crossed an Arrow table for every group in the file, and the unwanted ones were constructed, handed over the PyO3 boundary and discarded. The narrowing is now pushed down into the parse itself: asking for one group of 123 on a 25 MB file takes **131.2 ms instead of 144.4 ms (−9.1%)**, and the ~25 MB of Arrow tables nobody asked for is never allocated. A full read (`only_groups=None`, the default every existing caller takes) builds every group exactly as before. What it deliberately does **not** narrow is python-ags4's three hard raises — duplicate GROUP, ragged DATA row, and duplicate heading under `rename_duplicate_headers=False` — which read the whole file and still fire on an offence in a group the caller filtered out. Narrowing those too would turn a rejected file into an accepted one, so every group still carries its headings, line anchors and ragged list; only the table is conditional.

**The npm package's native loader reports a failed load properly, and understands `NAPI_RS_WASI_FLAVOR`.** `index.js` is generated by `@napi-rs/cli`, so a toolchain bump (3.7.4 → 3.8.2) rewrites it — and this one is not cosmetic. A load failure used to surface as whichever single error came last; it now builds a chain, each `Error` carrying the previous one as its `cause`, so "the addon would not load" finally tells you *which* of the candidate binaries failed and why. The WASI fallback also gained a flavour selector: `NAPI_RS_WASI_FLAVOR` picks a specific build and rejects an unknown value by name rather than silently ignoring it, and setting it now implies forcing WASI. Nothing in the loader's happy path changed — a successful `require('laterite')` resolves exactly as before.

**The bundled dictionary is stored once, not five times.** The five AGS4 editions overlap almost entirely — 89% of heading keys carry an identical definition in every edition they appear in — but the compiled tables held a complete copy per edition. They are now one set of tables keyed by the union, each key carrying one variant per *distinct* value plus a bitmask of the editions holding it. Nothing a consumer can observe changes: `dict_projection_pin` hashes every observable of every edition and reproduces all five digests exactly, which is why that test was written before the repack rather than after. Generated source drops 2,783,973 -> 906,008 bytes (-67%); the browser wasm drops 6.4% raw and 4.2% gzipped, which is 82 KiB off a gzipped payload. The gap between those two figures is the linker already deduplicating repeated string literals — what the repack removes is five copies of the table *structure*, not five copies of the strings.

fixed.text: **28 of the docs site's 30 admonitions rendered as an empty box.** Prettier de-indents the body of a `!!! note` / `??? tip`, and MkDocs needs that indentation to associate the body with the box — so the text escaped into a plain paragraph underneath while the titled box rendered empty. Because `prettier --check` is a CI gate, writing an admonition *correctly* meant failing the gate, which is why only two survived. The docs' Markdown is now outside prettier's scope (it is MkDocs-flavoured — admonitions, content tabs and `--8<--` includes are not prettier's dialect) and every body is re-indented; the built site now has zero empty admonition boxes.

**The release advisor recommended the wrong bump, in two different ways.** `gen_changelog.py --advise` is what `RELEASING.md` sends you to before stamping a version, and it disagreed with the policy paragraph in that same document. First, the pre-1.0 rule was applied in one place and not the other: `_bump()` correctly refused MAJOR at `0.x`, but the other branch escalated any non-empty `added` to MINOR regardless of version — so a documentation page would have cut a minor, which pre-1.0 *means* "something broke". Second, and worse, whether a change was breaking was decided by searching the entry prose for `\bbreaking\b`, which cannot tell a marker from a sentence denying one: "a non-breaking change" matched (the hyphen is a word boundary), as did "this is not a breaking change" and "avoids breaking downstream consumers". Every historical hit was a true positive only because the house style happened to be disciplined. Compatibility is now **declared** — `"breaking": true` on the entry — and the prose marker is kept as a cross-check the generator enforces in every mode: flag without marker, or marker without flag, fails. The six historical breaking entries are backfilled. The stakes are why: the engine tier publishes to crates.io, where a version can never be re-cut.

releases.summary: The Rust engine has an audience it did not have before: eight crates are on crates.io, and `laterite` is a real Rust API rather than a reserved name. That brought a second version number with it — the engine answers to `cargo add`, the products to `pip install` and `npm i` — so every surface now reports which ENGINE it carries, and the cross-surface gate checks it was comparing one. **Breaking:** the browser package finishes what 0.9.0 started — `diff` and `censor` take an options object like every other export, and `any` is gone from the `.d.ts` entirely.

added.text: **The browser package publishes its remaining result types, and `any` is gone from its `.d.ts` entirely.** `diff`, `dictionary` and `compute_fixes` were the three still returning `any`; they now return `RevisionDelta`, `StandardDict` and `Fix[]`, joining the shapes published previously. Consumers can delete their hand-written `RevisionDelta` / `StandardDict` / `Fix` / `SpanEdit` / `CellDelta` / `RowDelta` / `GroupDelta` / `DictGroup` / `DictHeading` mirrors — the validator site deleted ~120 lines of exactly those. Each new interface is bound to the Rust struct that serialises it by the same drift test as the others, and `Fix`'s `kind`/`risk` unions are checked against the validator's own enums, so a new fix kind cannot ship a `.d.ts` that lies about what you can receive.

**The fingerprint build refuses to emit a digest that covers too little.** It previously narrowed in silence — the dependency walk simply found nothing and carried on. It now fails the build, naming what it found. The existing coverage test cannot do this job: tests do not ship in a published crate, so the one build that had the defect was also the one build with nothing checking it.

**Three gates that have to work before the first crates.io publish, not after.** A published version's public API and its declared `rust-version` are both frozen, and the only remedy for either being wrong is a version bump every consumer has to follow. The new `publish-gates` CI job (1) builds the ten engine crates on the `rust-version` their own manifests declare, (2) diffs each crate's rendered public API against a checked-in snapshot under `tools/release/public-api/`, and (3) runs `cargo semver-checks` against `main`. The snapshot is the one that changes review: it puts the whole public surface into the PR's own diff, including the `Send`/`Sync` impls that are public API nobody writes down — an `Rc` in a private field silently removes `Send` from a consumer's type, and that is now a build failure rather than something a reviewer has to notice. Opaque `-> impl Trait` returns are the one thing a snapshot cannot see, so each is asserted at compile time instead, and the gate refuses to let a new one be added without one.

**The engine crates carry the metadata a crates.io page is made of.** `repository`, `keywords` and `categories` were absent, and seven of the eight round-one crates had no README. That is not a cosmetic gap: crates.io bakes metadata into the PUBLISHED VERSION, so adding it afterwards fixes future versions only — the pages for a version already on the registry would keep no link back to the source, permanently, and seven of them would have been a one-line description and nothing else. Each README is written to stand alone on the registry rather than assume the repository around it. The packaging gate caught all seven new files, which is what it is for.

**The eight round-one engine crates are armed for crates.io, and there is a tool that publishes them safely.** Every crate carried `publish = false` — a blanket safety catch, so `cargo publish` refused outright. It is now `true` on the eight; `laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` stay `false`, held for 0.2, with the reason recorded at the flag rather than somewhere a reader has to go looking. `tools/publish_crates.py` does the release: it derives the dependency waves from the manifests each run rather than restating them, waits for each wave to become RESOLVABLE from the registry (not merely uploaded — crates.io indexes on a delay, and a plain loop dies on wave 2 with wave 1 already permanently published), and is idempotent, so a re-run after a failure resumes instead of restarting. It refuses a dirty tree, any branch but `main`, a HEAD that is not `origin/main`, and any crate still marked `publish = false`. Nothing happens without `--execute`.

**The engine crates are on crates.io.** Eight of them at 0.9.0 — `laterite-ags4-parse`, `-types`, `-reference`, `-core`, `-validator`, `-emit`, `-trust` and `laterite-transport` — so a Rust consumer no longer needs a git dependency or a vendored path. `laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` are deliberately NOT published; they ship in 0.2, and the `publish = false` guard is what keeps that a decision rather than something to remember. `tools/publish_crates.py` gained `--through-wave N`, so a release can publish one wave, let the live pages be inspected, and only then commit the rest — worth the pause while metadata is still correctable on the crates that have not gone out.

**`laterite` — a Rust API, not just a facade.** The user-facing crate now exists and is functional at 0.1.0: read an AGS4 file from a path or bytes, walk its groups/headings/rows, edit cells and append rows, validate against the full numbered rule set, and write valid AGS4 back out. It carries its own version, deliberately — the engine crates are lockstep 0.9.x and reshape as the format work demands; this one is a different promise to a different audience. The design's central rule is now **mechanically enforced** rather than reviewed for: no third-party type may appear anywhere in its public API, checked against the rendered surface, so a `serde_json::Value` return or an `encoding_rs::Encoding` argument fails the build instead of silently binding our semver to a dependency's. `encoding_rs` is not even a dependency — encodings are WHATWG label strings. Held for 0.2, additively: diff, merge, typed cell access, indexed scan.

**`laterite` can validate bytes — `ags4::validate_bytes`, in 0.1.1.** 0.1.0 shipped `validate` taking a path only, which meant a service validating an upload had to give it a disk to sit on first. The reason written at the function — that Rule 20 is about files beside the `.ags`, so bytes could only answer half of it — did not hold: Rule 20 has been two modules since 2026-07-14, and `WorldScope` exists precisely to say which half ran, refusing the request with `WorldCheckRequiresSource` rather than reporting a clean Rule 20 nobody checked. Python, Node, wasm and the emitter were all already using it; the facade was the only surface that could not, and its error mapping already handled the token it never produced. Both arms now end at the engine's single door, so the edition resolved from `TRAN_AGS` and the 4.0.3→4.0.4 content guard cannot come out differently for one file read two ways — a test asserts exactly that, since it is the bug every hand-assembled surface has had. Asking for the on-disk check on bytes is an error, not a pass.

**Every surface can say which ENGINE it carries, not just which release it is.** `engine_fingerprint()` and `engine_version()` now exist on the wheel (`laterite.engine_fingerprint()`), the npm package (`engineFingerprint()`) and the browser build. The fingerprint is a build-time digest over every rule source, the dictionary and the rules catalogue, so it is the only value that can be believed: edit a rule and forget to bump anything and the semver is unchanged while the digest moves. Two surfaces reporting the same fingerprint ARE running the same rules; two reporting the same release number merely shipped together — a distinction this repo has already been burned by, when a compliance report hard-coded a version literal and kept printing it two minors after the workspace moved past it. It is also what an `.ags.idx` certificate stamps, so it is the right thing to quote in a bug report.

**The cross-surface gate now checks it was comparing the same engine.** `xcheck` holds eight surfaces to the in-process Rust authority's bytes, and half of those legs run against BUILT ARTEFACTS — a `wasm-pack` output, a tsup dist, an installed wheel — any of which can be stale while every case still matches, because a stale engine and a current one usually agree. The run then reports N-way identity across a surface compiled two weeks ago. Each leg now reports the engine fingerprint it is ACTUALLY running, asked of the artefact rather than assumed from the tree, and a mismatch against the authority's is a hard failure that the allowlist cannot excuse — an allowlisted engine split would be the gate agreeing to compare two different engines, which is the one thing it exists to refuse. A version number could not have done this job; the digest moves when a rule is edited even if nobody bumps anything. The three `cli-*` launcher legs have no door to ask through yet, so they are NAMED on stderr as unchecked rather than passed over, and the run reads as five identity-checked surfaces plus a known gap instead of a clean bill of health.

**All eight cross-surface legs now prove they were running the same engine — the three `lat` launchers included.** #204 gave five of them a fingerprint to compare and left `cli-native`, `cli-uvx` and `cli-npx` naming themselves as unchecked, because a launcher is a subprocess and none of the three would say what engine it carried. They say it now, through `lat census` — the hidden machine dump all three already implement and `tools/gen_census.py` already diffs them across. A second machine door would have been a second thing to keep in step, which is the failure the census exists to catch. `engine` is deliberately NOT a census table and is absent from `surface-census.json`: a fingerprint moves whenever a rule is edited, so snapshotting it would churn a checked-in file on every rule change while saying nothing about the surfaces. The schema version still bumped, because a launcher built before the field answers with it MISSING and missing is indistinguishable from a launcher with nothing to report — it would opt itself out of the identity check in silence. That version is hand-declared in four places and nothing had ever pinned them equal; a test now does, since a bump that reaches three of four makes the fourth launcher permanently "stale" to the generator, which reads as a build problem rather than the typo it is.

**A surface that stops reporting its engine now fails CI instead of printing a warning above a green run.** The cross-surface gate gained a second anti-rot switch, `--require-engines all`, alongside the `--require-legs all` it has always had — and for the same reason: the same silence means different things locally and on a runner. On your machine a leg that cannot name its engine is a fact about your working tree; in CI it means a surface dropped out of the identity check while the gate still said OK, which is the exact shape of a gate disarming itself. The nightly job now passes both. Neither `engine-mismatch` nor `engine-unreported` can be allowlisted — there is no finding to triage, because the comparison an entry would excuse did not happen between the things it claims — and adding an entry does not merely fail to help: the run then fails **twice**, because the entry also trips the allowlist's own staleness check.

**The npm package's error-mapping table is tested, and its coverage floors moved 93/84 → 97/89.** `errors.ts` is the module that turns an engine failure into the class callers branch on (`instanceof FileNotFoundError`, not a message match) — and nothing tested it; it was covered only incidentally by suites that happened to trip some of its arms. The new suite reads the error kinds OUT OF THE RUST SOURCE rather than restating them, because a third hand-list is the failure this repo keeps paying for: `ValidatorError::kind()` calls itself the single producer of that value domain and a new variant does force its Rust match, but nothing forced `makeError` to keep up — an unmapped kind falls through to a base `Ags4Error` with the right message and the right exit code, so every `instanceof` a caller wrote silently becomes false. Also covered: the four source shapes a handle can re-read (a path is re-read from DISK, not snapshotted, so certifying after an edit measures the current file), `certify`'s refusal to overwrite a file that is not a certificate, and the guards on `diff`/`fix`/`buildAgs4` that turn a mistake into a typed error instead of a raw `ENOENT` or a lookup on `undefined`.

**The browser bundle's least-tested module was the one standing between DuckDB values and the DOM.** `duckTypes.ts` calls itself "the single audited place" where an Int64 column's `bigint` and a TIMESTAMP's micros-since-epoch are normalised — rendering a bigint in JSX throws, and a micros value read as millis renders a plausible date in 1970 rather than an error — and it sat at 15% of lines. It now has a suite, as does `loadSensitive()` (whose fetch-once cache and non-OK-response guard decide whether the Anonymiser pre-ticks anything at all: a proxy's JSON error page would otherwise yield a document with no headings, and an anonymiser that redacts nothing while looking like it worked). The parent-chain walkers in `relationships.ts` gained tests for their cycle guards, which existed to stop a malformed dictionary freezing the tab and had never been exercised. The web lane also gained a BRANCH floor, which it never had — that absence is why the badge read ~85% while the lines gate sat green above 95, since a half-taken branch counts as a hit to lcov and a partial to Codecov. Generated wasm-pack glue is now excluded from the denominator so a local run and the CI run measure the same thing.

**The browser engine has a coverage figure for the first time — it was 69%, and nobody could see it.** `laterite-ags4-wasm` was the one shipped surface with no coverage gate of any kind. The nightly Rust job excludes it, correctly, because folding a binding cdylib into the ENGINE's denominator would move the engine's floor for reasons unrelated to the engine — but the exclusion read as "cannot be measured", and so nothing ever measured it. It was never unmeasurable: its 44 tests are plain `#[test]`s that `cargo test` runs on every PR. It now has its own nightly step, its own denominator and its own floor, deliberately separate so the engine's floor stays comparable run-to-run. Four exports whose signatures are plain Rust — `version`, `engine_version`, `engine_fingerprint`, `list_rules` — gained native tests; the two identity doors especially, since `engine_fingerprint` exists because a hard-coded constant once stood in for a real answer here, and a constant is exactly what these would silently become again. The ceiling is now stated rather than discovered: 103 of 218 functions are unreachable from a native test because they take or return JS types, so raising this means moving logic out of the fat `#[wasm_bindgen]` exports into plain functions, not writing more tests against the boundary.

**The npm surface reaches the 95% coverage bar, and its floors move 97/89 → 98/91.** Five suites, each aimed at a decision that fails *quietly*. The `0DP` → `BIGINT` arm of the AGS-type mapping had never been exercised — a count that arrives as `7.0` is a different fact from `7`, and it round-trips back out that way. `_filteredRows`' `WHERE TRUE` fallback and the `* EXCLUDE (_id, _parent_id)` choice both produce a query that *runs*, with the wrong rows or the wrong columns. And `ancestorChain`/`inheritedKeyNames` translate a native throw as `e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`, where only the first arm was ever taken: napi can surface a non-`Error`, and without the second arm the `Ags4Error` reports the string `"undefined"` — the only diagnostic the caller had, gone. `registry.ts` goes 50 → 100% branch. Falsified by mutation rather than by assertion count: censor's default inverted, the `TRUE`/`FALSE` clause flipped, the null-fill removed and the `String(e)` arm removed are all caught.
